utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I will now summarise the appeal and the manner in which we will proceed today. The case concerns the responsibility of Mr. Tolimir for crimes committed in Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves and in eastern Bosnia in 1995. At the time, Mr. Tolimir was an assistant commander in the chief of the sector for intelligence and security affairs of the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska or VRS. The Trial Chamber, Judge Nyambe dissenting, found that Tolimir participated in two joint criminal enterprises alleged in the indictment. A joint criminal enterprise, to murder the able-bodied men from the Srebrenica enclave, and a joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. The Trial Chamber by majority, Judge Nyambe dissenting, found Tolimir guilty -- the Trial Chamber by majority, Judge Nyambe dissenting, found Tolimir guilty pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal of genocide, conspiracy to commit genocide, extermination, murder, persecution, and inhumane acts through forcible transfer. The Trial Chamber, Judge Nyambe dissenting, sentenced Mr. Tolimir to life imprisonment. Mr. Tolimir advances 25 grounds of appeal, challenging his convictions and his sentence and requests that the Appeals Chamber reverse his convictions in their entirety or, in the alternative, significantly reduce his sentence. In grounds 1 through 4 of his appeal, Mr. Tolimir challenges the Trial Chamber's decision to take judicial notice of adjudicated facts and its evaluation of certain evidence. In ground 6 through 13, he challenges some of the Trial Chamber's legal and factual findings regarding extermination and forcible transfer as crimes against humanity. He further challenges the Trial Chamber's findings with respect to the crime of genocide. In grounds 15 and 14 through 20, Mr. Tolimir contests the majority's legal and factual findings concerning his responsibility for participation in the two joint criminal enterprises: That is the joint criminal enterprise to murder and the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove. In grounds 21 through 23, he challenges the majority's findings regarding his responsibility in relation to specific counts. Finally, in ground 24, Mr. Tolimir contests the majority's findings on his cumulative convictions, and in ground 25 its finding in relation to his sentence. The Prosecution responded that all grounds of Mr. Tolimir's appeal should be dismissed. I would like to draw the attention of the parties to the matters that the Appeals Chamber invited the parties in the addendum to the scheduling order to discuss. This addendum was filed on 31 October, 2014. Throughout the hearing, counsel may argue the grounds of appeal in any order they consider suitable. Throughout the hearing, counsel may argue the grounds of appeal in any order they consider suitable for their presentation. However, I would urge counsel not to repeat or summarise the arguments presented in their briefs. The Appeals Chamber is familiar with these arguments. Furthermore, the parties are obliged to provide precise references to materials supporting their oral arguments. The Judges, of course, may interrupt the parties at any time to ask questions or they may ask questions following each party's submissions or at the end of the hearing. I would also like to remind the parties to be particularly careful not to reveal any information that could identify a protected witness or other protected information. Finally, I reiterate that the appeal process is not a trial de novo and the parties must refrain from repeating their cases presented at trial. Arguments must be limited to alleged errors of law which invalidate the trial judgement or alleged rules of fact which occasion a miscarriage of justice. As set out in the Scheduling Order, this hearing will proceed as follows. First, we will hear submissions from legal advisor from Mr. Tolimir for two hours. After the lunch break, the Prosecution will respond for two hours. After a pause of 20 minutes, legal advisor for Mr. Tolimir will have 30 minutes to reply. Finally, Mr. Tolimir will have ten minutes for a personal address if he wishes to do so. Having now stated the manner in which we will proceed, I would invite the legal advisor for Mr. Tolimir to make submissions. Mr. Gajic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, esteemed members of the Appeals Chamber, it is my honour and with great responsibility to appear here before you today, particularly in the case which falls in the category of serious Srebrenica cases which raises a plethora of disputable facts and legal issues.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Gajic please try to read more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That may have an impact on the final outcome of this case. Due to the time limitation of two hours that I have, the entire submission or the great part thereof will be dedicated to the questions posed by the Appellate Chamber Judges that were contained in the addendum to the Scheduling Order and which are -- enter the core of the very case. Before I start giving answers to the Judges' questions, I would like to say that this appeal's procedure is particularly difficult because members of the Appeals Chamber have taken diametrically opposing views not only on one legal criteria or they were in disagreement about one or two facts but rather Judge Nyambe expressed a dissenting opinion portraying a completely different picture to the one established by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You mean the Trial Chamber, not the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. President. Now I'm going to begin with the answers posed by the Appeals Chamber and I will follow the order in which they were posed in the addendum for the Scheduling Order. The first question of the Chamber is regarding appeals ground 7 and 10 is whether the operations of the Bosnian Serbs in Zepa were acts of genocide, if they are perceived separately from the killing in Srebrenica. The position of the appellant is even though they are perceived either separately or together with the acts concerning Srebrenica, the operations of the Bosnian Serbians in Zepa cannot be considered as acts of genocide because there is no exhibit on record that would serve as a proper basis to conclude that there was an intent of genocide on the population. There is not a single act that would constitute genocide. There were no killings, there were no infliction of heavily bodily harm or mental harm or placing the whole group under the conditions that were conducive to its destruction. Ground 7 concerns an error of law and it considers the questions whether forcible transfer can be considered as genocide according to Article 4(2) of the Statute and whether there was erroneous finding as stated in appeals ground number 10, among others, which state that genocide was committed in Zepa. The transfer of population as such cannot be considered as an act of genocide. There was some proposals during the drafting of the genocide convention to qualify it as genocide. Professor Bartos, who represented Yugoslavia in these negotiations, invoked the case of the relocation of the Slav population during the Second World War which was carried out by the Nazis, the relocation of the population as qualified equal to intentional destruction of a group. It was concluded that the genocide may be considered by forcing members of the groups to abandon their genocide. This proposal was made by Syria, it was supported by Yugoslavia, but eventually it was rejected by a great majority, 22 votes against, five for, and eight abstained with the explanation that it is far too separate from the concept of genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I don't understand the -- you said it was concluded that the genocide may be considered by forcing members of the groups to abandon their genocide. You meant "perpetrators" or "victims"? Are you speaking of abandoning their places of abode or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so. To abandon their place of residence or to be forcibly relocated from the places where they had been living before. Here of course I'm talking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay. So not to abandon their genocide but to abandon their places of residence. That's what I thought. Okay. It's clear now. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course it seems that I need to speak slowly because I have to wait for quite some time to see on the screen the interpretation of what I am saying. The Trial Chamber, however, when it classified forcible relocation of population as a serious mental impairment in keeping with Article 4 of the Statute relied on the draft convention on genocide which can be seen in footnote of the judgement 3107 in which the notion of a genocide is defined in a totally different way than in the Statute of the Tribunal and the convention on the prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide which probably alleged to the fact that in its analysis, it separated from the concept of genocide as exists in the applicable international law and to provide a totally different definition of serious mental harm. Let me remind you, the Chamber, that this kind of mental harm decided that it is a harm which is not so serious as the temporary resentment, anxiety, or humiliation. It does -- we need not have permanent consequences or that cannot be or may not be irreversible but that it inflicted long-term and serious impairment on the ability of an individual to lead a normal and constructive life. This definition of mental harm is in keeping with the part of the definition that is contained in the convention draft which was later on deleted and which in addition to the applicable definition of genocide and a criminal act against the prevention -- protection of group in order for its gradual or partial destruction added the following: In order to prevent its prevention and development, according to international law the prevention of preservation and development of group is not an element of genocide. [B/C/S spoken] ... of the convention on genocide indicated the notion of mental harm found its place in the convention at the proposal of China which in explaining its proposal made reference to the acts committed by the Japanese occupation forces against the Chinese population by the use of narcotic and cited that although they were not so spectacular as mass killings in gas chambers in Nazi Germany, its result is not less lethal. Pages 59 to 60. In terms of the convention on genocide, a notion of serious mental harm cannot be considered as harm that makes an individual unable to lead a normal and constructive life but it has to be serious enough in order to pose a threat to a total or partial destruction of a group as understood by biological or physical survival. This interpretation, which we stated in our brief, is further supported by a declaration proposed by the US to the instrument on the ratification of the Convention on Genocide believing that mental harm is only, and I quote, "permanent impairment of mental facilities through drugs, torture, and similar techniques." There is no doubt that genocide, as the most serious crime recognised by international law, provides protection of the existence of a national, racial, religious, or ethnic group as such. If we look at the whole of the convention and if we interpret it in the preparatory work for adopting it, what is added to the killing - that is to say, infliction of serious mental or physical injuries or placing it in such condition that it leads to its destruction - cannot be considered as the accomplishment of the final effect but rather that it has elements of an act that has as its aim the final and eventual destruction of a group. The position of the Defence is that the forcible relocation can be considered to be an act of genocide only if it is done in a manner that may be qualified as grievous mental harm or place in the group in conditions that are conducive to its destruction such as the forcible relocation to concentration camps, ghettos, or areas in which they are exposed to plight, enslavement, and in which the conditions that pervade are equal to degradation, denial of their human rights, and generally the conditions that lead to the destruction of the group. However, we understand the notion of mental harm of placing a group under the conditions that lead to its destruction. Not a single act that I described committed by the Army of Republika Srpska in Zepa cannot be qualified as genocide. The majority of Trial Chamber members, in paragraphs 758 of the judgement, reached the conclusions that no reasonable trier of fact would have received and that is that the serious mental injuries inflicted on Bosnian Muslims who were forcibly moved from Zepa in the period between 25th and 27th July, 1995. First of all, there is no evidence that can confirm that there was a genocidal intent with regard to the Bosnian Muslims of Zepa. Secondly, the act that the Trial Chamber reviewed when reaching its conclusion cannot be classified as acts of genocide. I would like to remind you, and this is going to be the subject of discussion regarding some other questions posed by the Judges of the Appeals Chamber, is that the genocidal intention in the view of the Trial Chamber is primarily based on the operation of killing. In the course of the operation of Zepa, there was no killing of POWs of Zepa, nor was the civilian population exposed to killings. The third amended indictment does not contain any allegations about Zepa. And speaking about the case of the killing of Palic, Hajric, and Imamovic, I will deal with this later on in response to the second question of the Trial Chamber. Zepa fell only after three rounds of notions in which in every case a population was offered a possibility to stay in Zepa. As explained in appeals ground 1,5 paragraph 303 to 328 of the consolidated appeal brief, I would like to remind you of some of the facts which confirm the submission that an attack on Zepa and the mode of conducting a military operation in Zepa was not illegal. In an order to attack Zepa, General Krstic clearly stated that the civilian and Muslim population and UNPROFOR are not the target of our operation. This is P1225, page 4, and in judgement it's paragraph 1028, footnote 4061. An attack on Zepa is a reaction to the attempt by the Muslims to link the enclaves with a central part of the territory under the BH control through military operations and by launching frequent attacks from the enclaves. The exhibits that confirm this are listed in paragraph 306 of the appellate brief. These attacks resulted in great casualties among the Serbian army and population which was confirmed by the Trial Chamber. The absence of the genocide intent can be further corroborated by the documents of the UN. I would particularly like to refer to P596, paragraph 9, which says, I quote: "The Serbs want to occupy the pocket of Zepa without any fighting, if possible." Describing the meeting of 13 July in which Tolimir participated, it is said that "Serbs asked the Bosnian from Zepa to lay down their arms after which the civilian population can stay or go." Paragraph 8 of the document. In other words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the very commencement of the attack on Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. The first issue raised in the addendum to the Scheduling Order raised the question of the nexus or not nexus between the operations in Zepa and those in Srebrenica. In the -- your appeal brief at paragraph 164, you argued that the Trial Chamber was required to analyse separately the operations of the Bosnian Serb army in Srebrenica and in Zepa. And this relates, of course, to the operative indictment which in this case defined the targeted group that is the subject of the charges against Mr. Tolimir as, and I quote, "Muslim population of eastern Bosnia," eastern Bosnia. According to the indictment, this constituted part of the Bosnian population as a whole. Can you explain to us why was the Trial Chamber required, as you allege, to analyse separately the operations in Srebrenica and in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the operation in Zepa was led under completely different circumstances to those of the operation in Srebrenica. The differences are obvious, beginning with how it began, how it developed, the way the negotiations were conducted, and everything else. As far as the attack on Zepa is concerned, it absolutely lacks the features that existed in the attack in Srebrenica, although the Defence believes that both operations were completely lawful. Second, the Defence asserts that the Muslim population of the whole eastern Bosnia was not a target of attack, neither in Srebrenica nor in Zepa. However, two different operations can be qualified in a different manner, legally. Establishing genocidal intent, the Trial Chamber stated that it encompassed the entire population of the eastern Bosnia. The Defence claims that it did not, neither in Srebrenica nor in Zepa. In order to reach such a finding, it has to be established separately whether the civilian population of Srebrenica was exposed to acts that constitute genocide separately from the population of Zepa. In Zepa there was no genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the position of the Defence that not only there is no proof that the civilian population was a target of attack but also that it was not the ambition of the VRS to remove the population from Zepa forcibly. This is shown by the meetings of 13, 19, and 24 July, as well as the agreements that had been reached and that Bosnian Muslims did not honour. Every time an agreement was reached, they wanted to cheat their way out of it. The Trial Chamber in its reasoning in which it found that the forcible transfer of population from Zepa constitutes an act of genocide relied on several controversial findings. First of all, in paragraph 758 of the judgement it emphasised that the transport of the population from Zepa unfolded in somewhat different circumstances than the transport of Muslims from Srebrenica. First of all, the population of Zepa was transported to the territory in which an identical national, racial, religious, and ethnic group resided that was under the control of the government which they considered to owe loyalty to and in which they were not exposed to circumstances conducive to their destruction. The very transport was executed, as found by the Trial Chamber, with the escort of UNPROFOR, with the listing of the names of all those transported, which was done by the local Muslims and UN representatives, and there was also an order by Mladic that Muslims transported may not be maltreated and nothing may be taken away from them. That is P2427. The Trial Chamber as an element in its reasoning that serious mental harm was inflicted, stated that on 20th July the population was invited by public announcement to return to the enclave. Let me recall that the Chamber established that this public announcement was ordered by Tolimir, which is indisputable and established in paragraph 61 of the judgement. The Trial Chamber erred when relying on this fact in finding whether the population of Zepa suffered grievous bodily harm. Inviting the population on the 20th of July to return to the enclave followed after the agreement of 19 July between Mladic, a representative of the War Presidency, parliamentarians, Torlak and Kulovac, were the representatives of the War Presidency of Zepa expressed their readiness to lay down their arms, to surrender them, and agreed on the evacuation of the civilian population. Also the evidence shows that ten entire families wanted to stay in the enclave, that's D58. Inviting the population to return to Zepa after the agreements were reached with parliamentarians from Zepa, although it may have been unpleasant for some civilians, certainly does not have the character of mental injury. Also the Trial Chamber when explaining its qualification of forcible transfer as serious mental harm, states that Tolimir's conduct while -- is an element in this, his conduct in Zepa during the evacuation. The Trial Chamber relied on the evidence of one witness, David Wood, who cannot be considered as a reliable witness as explained in the consolidated appeals brief in paragraph 153 and the amended reply in paragraph 53. This witness said that Tolimir contributed to a threatening atmosphere by going through the masses of people with his gun pointed in the air. Other witnesses, Edward Joseph and Zoran Carkic, testified about the way about the way in which the evacuation of the civilian population from Zepa was conducted about which Mr. Wood had no particular knowledge how it was organised and especially how Tolimir behaved during that time. Two witnesses of the Prosecution, Edward Joseph and Zoran Carkic, confirmed that Tolimir did not have any arms while in Zepa. In fact, he was not seen carrying any weapons. Edward Joseph does not remember Tolimir having any weapons while Carkic, in an interview with the Prosecution, emphasised: "He came unarmed and amongst the thousands of civilian population and before I went in." He testified that Tolimir insisted, "Nothing should happen to the people," D217, page 13 and 14. Not a single reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Tolimir's behaviour in Zepa constitutes infliction of mental harm or contributed to infliction of mental harm. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber cites as a ground for its finding that serious mental harm was inflicted certain situations during the evacuation from Zepa in which Mladic gets on each of the buses and addresses the population evacuated from Zepa. They take out of context several expressions such as "I give you your life as a gift," without viewing them in the context of this address. They take a few words out of context which would not be done by any reasonable trier of fact. In the file we have a video and the transcript of Mladic's entry into the buses, P1740. For example, in one of the buses Mladic said: "Our children were killed too in 1992 in the Zepa canyon. You heard about me. Now you are watching me. I am General Mladic. There are able-bodied men among you. All of you are safe and you will be transported to Kladanj. I wish you a safe journey and goodbye." That is P1740, 2631. He also said: "Among you there are militarily-able people who shot at me. I forgive you all and I give you your life as a gift. Do not come before me on the front line. Next time there will be no forgiveness. I have mercy for you as you did not have any for our children in 1992 in the Zepa canyon. Safe trip and goodbye." That is again P1740, pages 2641. Such statements could not be interpreted by any reasonable trier of fact as elements corroborating the theory about the infliction of serious mental harm. These reasons are sufficient to point out to the errors made by the Trial Chamber in finding that the transfer of population from Zepa have any features of an act of genocide or that the operations of the VRS in Srebrenica constitute acts of genocide or were done with genocidal intent. The second question from the Appeals Chamber concerns ground of appeal number 2; namely, did the Trial Chamber err in finding that the forces of Bosnian Serbs killed Mehmet Hajric, Amir Imamovic, and Avdo Palic with a particular intent to destroy part of the Bosnian Muslim population as such. I would like to recall, first of all, that in the judgement of the Trial Chamber in the Krstic case, it is clearly emphasised that intent has to be indisputably unambiguously established from factual circumstances of the criminal act charged in the indictment as well as that the conditions of the existence of evidence of particular intent and indications that the whole group or a considerable part of the group was designated for destruction. These standards prevent an easy conviction for genocide. The criminal act of genocide by its very nature requires intent to destroy at least a considerable, that is significant, part of a group. The killing of three Muslims from Zepa, regardless of their position they had as members of the War Presidency in Zepa, does not meet this standard. Genocide is not an act, is not a crime against an individual or several individuals but against a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group. As stated in paragraph 9 of the appeals judgement in Krstic, Ralph Lemkin stressed that when partial destruction is concerned in order for the standard of genocide to be met, it has to be a significant part of the group; that is to say, a large number of individuals belonging to that group such that it affects the whole of the group. The Trial Chamber was guided by one criterion alone invoked by the Trial Chamber in the case of Jelisic, citing the report of the commission of experts stating that in a situation in which essentially the target is the entire leadership of the group, including political and administrative leaders, religious leaders, academicians, and intellectuals, prominent business and other people, this can also constitute genocide and that totality in itself can be a strong indication of genocide regardless of the number of those killed. The Appeals Chamber in the Krstic case criticised the findings from Jelisic and Sikirica taking the position that if a certain part of the group in one or another way constitutes a whole group or if it is of key importance to its survivor, it can support the argument that this part is qualified as significant for the purposes of Article 4 of the Statute. However, this factor does not stand alone. It is just one of the indications of whether the standard of significance is met. In the Krstic case the Appeals Chamber did not deal in greater deal with this criterion. However, we believe that this criterion can be an indicator of genocide only if it is part of a policy that is systematically pursued as one of the stages in pursuing the genocidal plan. In the appeals brief in paragraph 183, we cited the opinion of Professor Kreca, that is a judge of the International Court of Justice who in his separate opinion in the case Bosnia-Herzegovina versus Yugoslavia, indicated that the concept of "leader" is not sufficiently clear and that it leads through the backdoor a consideration of leaders as a separate protected object of the convention on genocide of which there is no trace neither in the preparatory work nor in the draft of the convention. It also states that the concept of leader in modern society for human freedoms and rights has an accronis [phoen] and discriminatory connotation which runs counter to the ideas that constitute a foundation for human rights of individuals and groups. For establishing genocidal intent, one of the factors that is important is also the moment in time when they were killed. In the case of Palic, that was 4 or 5 September. While it is quite certain that Imamovic and Hajric were alive in August 1995 and in the period when they were probably killed and the circumstances of their killing have not been established. The Trial Chamber considered the fact that the alleged forcible transfer of the population of Zepa happened before their killing. It qualifies it as a factor corroborating the finding of genocidal intent, paragraph 781. This is a finding that would not be made by any reasonable Trial Chamber; namely, the fact that they were killed as confirmed by forensic reports after the population left Zepa shows that their importance to that community was not the same anymore even if they had been of key importance to the survival of one small community. However, neither that community in 1995 was very small anymore nor can anything suggest the conclusion of the majority of the Trial Chamber that it constituted several thousand people. Before the war it was less than 3.000 and during the war the Trial Chamber established the number to be between 6.500 and 10.000. The ABiH in Zepa was defeated. There was no need anymore to organise civilian protection. There was no need for the work of the War Presidency in Zepa. In any case, they were not of key importance to the survival of Muslims from Zepa. At the time of their killing, the Muslim population of Zepa was already on the territory of BH or in Serbia. Furthermore, there is reference to the killing of three persons who were taken as prisoners of war in a lawful manner after the fall of Zepa and who, considering that they were captured, could not have any role in the enclave. Therefore, their murder does not fit the standard formulated by the Trial Chamber as "intentional destruction of a limited number of persons selected for their influence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. What did you mean by saying that they were killed in a lawful manner?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I never said that they were killed in a lawful manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: It's maybe a problem with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were taken prisoner in a lawful manner. And since they were taken prisoner, they could not have any influence on the enclave and life in it. That's why their killing does not meet the standard that was formulated by the Trial Chamber as the intentional destruction of a limited number of persons selected because of the influence that they have and that they could have on the survival of a group as such. Their killing did not have any influence on the survival of the group nor could a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that it had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can see that the interpretation is very slow and I'm reading very fast in the Serbian language. That's why I'm going to slow down and I am going to skip a few of the arguments, but I would like to remind everybody that in our appeal brief we pointed to the fact that based on the agreement on the militarisation, Avdo Palic as the commander of the Zepa Brigade should not have been in the enclave in the first place and that Imamovic and Hajric participated in combat and that combat was launched from the enclave which was explained in paragraphs 179 through 910 in the appeals hearing. But I would also like to point to the fact that the report of Viktor Bezruchenko, which is D21, paragraph 12, who was an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor, points to the fact that they were not very crucial for the survival of a small community. He points to the fact that those people who were in Zepa who were intellectuals and who could have organised life in Zepa tried to leave Zepa instead. Delic wrote an appeal, according to Bezruchenko, and said that one of the causes of the departure of the population was mistrust in the leadership structures which were at odds. And now we come to another thing in the reasoning of the Trial Chamber which tries to say that, as corroboration to the genocidal intention, was that Hajric and Imamovic were separated from the other prisoners of war. However in different place in the judgement, we see Tolimir's instruction on the way how prisoners of war should be classified, and he quotes that as an example of the fact that Tolimir was aware of the international law relative to treating prisoners of war. We'll find that in paragraph 1122 of the judgement. Document P134, which is a Prosecutor's exhibit, testifies to Tolimir's instructions on treating prisoners of war in Rasadnik. On page 5 of this document, its author, Carkic, reports: "In keeping with the order issued by General Tolimir and his instructions, all the necessary measures were taken in accordance with possibilities." Inter alia, he also points to the fact that prisoners of war were classified and that healthy prisoners were accommodated in one room, the wounded and sick in another room, and in the third room they put members of the former leadership. It says "Atlantida," and that's a reference to Avdo Palic is in a different location and his accommodations is better. And now "efendija," meaning Hajric, is approved to pray in his room five times a day. And there is a reference to the food, medical treatment, and particularly important is the fact that Tolimir instructed that they should be registered with the International Committee of the Red Cross. The fact that they were kept in a separate room cannot be taken as corroboration for the argument that they were killed with a genocidal intention. And finally when it comes to the reason, motives, and intentions behind the killings of Palic, Hajric, and Imamovic, very little is known about all that. There is not enough proof. However, what was said by a member of the VRS, Zoran Carkic, who was an officer of the Rogatica Brigade at the time, is that Palic, Hajric, and Imamovic participated in the armed combat in Zepa including the participation in the massacre of imprisoned soldiers, Serbs, in 1992. I would like to refer you to T 12787 page in the transcript. In the absence of any proof of the circumstances of their death, who, when, and why they killed them, one cannot arrive at a reliable conclusion that they were killed with a genocidal intention. And the thesis that they may have been killed because they had participated in combat operations, for example, in the killing of those who were injured and sick in 1992 in the Zepa canyon may be considered a reliable and well grounded thesis. However, it is a more reasonable conclusion than the conclusion of the Trial Chamber, that they were killed because of their leadership position and because of the influence that they had on the entire group of Bosnian Muslims in Zepa. I would like to move on to question number 3 posed by the Appeals Chamber, and it reads: "In connection with the appeals grounds 14 and 16, did the Trial Chamber err where it relied on, inter alia, Tolimir's position of the chief of the sector for intelligence and security affairs and in his professional control over subordinate intelligence and security organs when they concluded that under 1, Tolimir knew that his subordinates participated in the joint criminal enterprise to kill people, and under 2, that he intended himself to participate in the joint criminal enterprise to kill people?" Could I please be informed as to how long do I have before our first break? I would like to adjust my presentation accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Of course all of this is stated in the Scheduling Order and the present stage of your presentation should end at 11.15 and then we will have a pause of 20 minutes and then we will -- you will have from 11.35 until 12.20. And so please try to schedule your presentation in such a way as to have time to cover all the principal points and take into account that my colleagues may want to ask for some questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. President. I just needed to know whether there would be any delays due to the delay at the start. The Trial Chamber did not err when it said that Tolimir knew that certain persons participated in the JCE and with respect to the fact that he intended to participate in the JCE. An important determinant of all these findings was the -- Tolimir's position in the VRS including his relationship with General Mladic who was the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. To what extent did these findings influence the conclusions of the Trial Chamber is seen from the dissenting opinion of Judge Nyambe in paragraph 4. I'm not going to quote all of it, but the Trial Chamber also says that in a number of paragraphs at the beginning of the judgement, for example, in paragraph 115 of the judgement, a majority of the members of the Trial Chamber points to the fact that when arriving at the conclusion that the accused was a participant in both JCEs, a majority of the Trial Chamber members took into account the functions and the authorities of the accused and erred when it concluded that the accused had reliable communication channels via his subordinates and that he was regularly informed on what was going on in the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, that he was one of Mladic's associates that Mladic relied on and trusted, that he was his second in command and his right hand, based on the description provided by General Smith and his conclusion that they were almost equal, and it was often mentioned that Tolimir was Mladic's eyes and ears as it were. The first thing that I would like to draw your attention to in my presentation is the fact that the Trial Chamber fully confused several categories that concerned the control and command of the army. As was explained in the appeals brief, and I'm not going to repeat that portion, when it comes to leadership or rather the direction and command of certain organs, sometimes implying the full control of their work including issuing certain orders as to what needed to be done. Popovic, Momir Nikolic, and other members of the intelligence sector are erroneously mentioned in the judgement as those who were subordinated to Tolimir. However, such a situation is not sustainable and is not in accordance with the evidence adduced. What I would like to mention at this moment is the fact that there is no proof that Tolimir in the relevant period of time, while all those killings were taking place in the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade and the Zvornik Brigade, received any reports on any killings on any criminal intent or plan. In practical terms, the conclusions of the Trial Chamber boiled down to the following: If somebody of those whom we consider to have been subordinated to Tolimir participated in the killings, Tolimir should have known about that. If he spoke to somebody, we are certain that such a message was conveyed to him. However, this way of evaluating evidence, and I've simplified things very much because of the constraints of time, is contrary to what should be done in evaluating judgements as demonstrated by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 98 of the Krstic judgement. It says: "Despite the claim of the Trial Chamber that if General Mladic knew of the killing, Krstic should have known about them as well." The Trial Chamber did not establish based to Krstic's contacts with General Mladic during that period of time that Radislav Krstic really learned in those context about the intention to have Bosnian Muslims killed. The claim by the Trial Chamber did not have valid probative grounds. No reasonable trier of fact if they did not really establish that Krstic was aware of General Mladic's intention would draw an inference that Krstic shared that intention and that knowledge. Unlike the Krstic case, as I'm going to explain in some more detail later on, a majority of the members of the Trial Chamber placed most of the weight to the fact that the relationship between Tolimir and Mladic was good, that Mladic trusted Tolimir, that in the absence of any proof on the communication between Tolimir and members of the intelligence and security organs during the relevant period, that it would be inconceivable if Tolimir had not been aware of the operation to kill people. Now what did the Trial Chamber particularly rely on while reviewing this finding concerning the knowledge on Tolimir's part about the operation of killings as well as Tolimir had intended to take part in it and that he had contributed to it. First of all, in paragraph 1096, on the 13th of July Tolimir was in the area of Zepa and in the following days he was intensively engaged in the area by participating in the negotiations about the evacuation of the Bosnian Muslims. The alleged operation of killings is relating to the period from 12 or 13 July until 19th of July. We believe that to be a relevant period in which it has to be established that Tolimir was aware of the operation of the killings. The Trial Chamber by invoking document D64, sent by Tolimir after 2200 hours on the 12th of July, concluded that at the time when it was issued he had not known anything about the plan to kill the Muslims of Srebrenica. However, the Chamber relying on Tolimir's relationship with Mladic - and there is no evidence that Tolimir was in Fontana Hotel during the negotiations or that he was in Srebrenica ever, for that matter - when Tolimir said that all able-bodied men who are evacuated from Potocari should be recorded and listed, the Trial Chamber says that this coincides with what Mladic had said about searching, or rather, screening whether among the POWs there were those who committed certain crimes. This document, this D64, reads in its relevant part: "Bearing in mind that it is very important to arrest as many members of Muslim formations as possible, or to execute them if they offer resistance, it is also necessary to record all able-bodied men who are evacuated from the base in Potocari," which means to make a list of all of them. There is no search for prisoners of war. Tolimir believes and he thinks that they shouldn't be separated at all. However, in order to understand this proposal and this proposition, it is necessary to look at the whole of this document. Tolimir says that the Muslims want to portray Srebrenica as being demilitarised and that only civilians were there. For that reason, it was ordered that all armed able-bodied men to illegally pull out of the territory of Republika Srpska to the territory under the Muslim control in order to accuse the VRS that it had attacked the civilian population in a safe zone without any cause whatsoever. The only reasonable conclusion that can be derived from this document is that Tolimir wanted to provide evidence that there were military forces stationed in Srebrenica and to deny all the accusations that the attack on the zone was launched while it was populated only by the civilians. However, based on this document, D64, the Chamber concluded that even though Tolimir -- or rather, the Chamber concluded that Tolimir did not know about the operational killing but that he was in contact with all the relevant personnel and organs and that he was kept abreast about the developments in Srebrenica. However, there is no evidence that Tolimir from the evening of 12th July onwards was informed about the developments in Srebrenica. Based on Mladic's order, Tolimir was in Zepa at the time. On the 13th of July, a document was produced which we find to be extremely disputable. It's P125. And it is allegedly authored by General Savcic who also was in Zepa on the 13th of July. The Defence believes that this document is not authentic and we provided reasons for that in our appeals brief. However, what is in dispute in weighing the evidence and when establishing the authenticity is the fact that the Trial Chamber did not rely on the testimony of General Savcic who was in Zepa at the time with quite a small number of soldiers but rather on the testimony of Mr. Blaszczyk who was the Prosecutor's investigator. Among other things, the testimony of the Prosecutor's investigator provides denial on the existence of the forward command post of the 65th Protection Regiment. However, Mr. Blaszczyk has no military expertise and he has no knowledge on these matters. When analysing this document, the Trial Chamber also omitted to note certain things, which is that this document does not contain anything that might point to something dubitable or something that no other army in the world would have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You have argued, Counsel, that Mr. Tolimir was not aware of the plan to kill the males, Bosnian males, Bosniak males. Could you explain, then, why did he propose that those persons, the males, be put in a closed hangar to avoid detection? This, of course, appears from Defence Exhibit 49. Was this an order to hide, to cover up for the killings?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in this period between the 12th July and onwards, we are talking about something that everybody saw, UNPROFOR, there was testimony that TV crews were there who filmed them. Nobody was trying to conceal the existence of POWs. I believe that what this is about is usual practice, to put the prisoners inside certain facilities in order to guard them better and also to prevent others from seeing these prisoners of war. However, there is one more thing. In that period, the VRS was under the threat of NATO bombing. I believe that this is not the case of hiding POWs but rather of undertaking usual measures of caution. Not to kill them. There were other officers, like Tolimir, who testified here. Tolimir was a smart and competent officer. Can we then assume if such an officer, knowing that UNPROFOR was passing by and if everybody was aware of the existence of POWs would order for these prisoners to be hidden away in order to kill them later on? There is no evidence whatsoever proving that Tolimir knew at all about any plans about the murder from other generals. Nobody can say that this document represents something that is unlawful. I'm sorry. I just looked in the transcript. Maybe I didn't hear. You asked me about document D49, which is a document in which Tolimir informs about the existence of accommodation facility for 800 prisoners of war in the area of the Rogatica Brigade. In our opinion, this document shows that Tolimir had no knowledge about the murders operation or about the intention to kill them. In this document, D49, Tolimir says, "If you're not able to provide proper accommodation for all POWs...," and this specific expression reveals that Tolimir was not in charge of providing accommodation. He's just speaking about accommodation. And then he says "proper accommodation," and we understand this to be only such accommodation that satisfied all the requirements stated in Geneva Conventions, particularly the third one. This document especially negates that Tolimir was aware of the murder operation at the time and that he intended to contribute to it, and especially it is impossible to interpret this document as something that represents something that is contributing to the JCE of the murder of Bosnian Muslims. Tolimir was in Zepa at the time. We have evidence given by Zoran Carkic who described how this document was drafted and when it was sent. However, we have no evidence as to what was subsequently done about it. Probably nothing. There were no preparations because obviously his information about the existence of this accommodation facility was just noted but it was not taken into consideration. Another element that I would like to underlie here in the Trial Chamber's reasoning relates to a document that Tolimir sent -- or rather, received from the Main Staff and he forwarded it to the Drina Corps. In this document, it is stated that there is a drone in the air and that certain measures need to be taken. The Trial Chamber concluded that because of his function, which means to prevent the leakage of intelligence, did this in order to conceal the killings that were already taking place in the area of Zvornik. We consider this kind of reasoning to be totally erroneous. There is no indication whatsoever that this was done in order to hide the killings, whereas at the time preparations for an attack on Zepa were being made and the Zvornik Brigade was still engaged in military operations. Not a single reasonable trier of fact could conclude that this was issued in order to contribute to the JCE of murders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that this may be a good time for us to have a pause of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Before starting, I would like to congratulate the interpreters for a heroic performance and you will have not to go too fast and yet you know we operate under strict time limits. So it is your turn again, continued submission by Tolimir, 45 minutes. You know that usually the shorter the presentation the more effective it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely agree with you, Mr. President. Regarding the issues we are dealing with now, I wish to point out certain errors of the Trial Chamber concerning the way it evaluated the evidence. Let us take the example of a communication that Tolimir had with Popovic on the 22nd of July, 1995. If I'm not mistaken it's the only communication that Tolimir had at the time with Popovic. Popovic is making inquiries about a relative of his, Tolimir says he cannot do anything, he asks what's going on, what he's doing, and Tolimir says, "Do your job." These words, "do your job," are cited by both the OTP and the Trial Chamber to conclude that it has something to do with the killings in Bisina. These killings in Bisina, as well as those on the 16th of July in Branjevo, according to the findings of the Trial Chamber, were carried out by the 10th Sabotage Detachment. However, this 10th Sabotage Detachment was not commanded by Tolimir. It was not even commanded by Salapura. It was directly subordinated to the commander of the Main Staff. And in the evidence of Salapura, this detachment could have been used without Tolimir or Salapura knowing anything about it. It was an independent unit of the VRS. Tolimir and Salapura had certain competences only with regard to the training of that detachment and could propose appointments to it, and the very fact that Tolimir talked to Popovic on the 22nd and the supposition that he talked to Salapura on the 16th or communicated by telegram or in some other way is insufficient to conclude that Tolimir was informed of the murder operation. That is simply going one step too far and indicates what I pointed out earlier regarding the way evidence was evaluated as the Appeals Chamber also emphasised in the Krstic case. Regarding the issue of whether Tolimir was aware of the murder operation and whether he intended to participate it in and whether he contributed to it, the Trial Chamber found that Tolimir allegedly failed in his duty to protect the prisoners of war from Srebrenica. What does the Trial Chamber proceed from? They proceed from the supposition that Tolimir played a role in the exchange of POWs. That's paragraph 1122 of the judgement. And from that, they draw the conclusion of his duty to protect POWs. Exchange is basically paperwork. It does not imply "care about the treatment of POWs." POWs have to be treated by everyone in a lawful way, that obligation is indisputable. But the powers and the duty to treat POWs properly lie with the units that captured them and held them. Tolimir is at that time in Zepa and he received no authorisation or no instruction or obligation to take care of the prisoners from Srebrenica from Mladic or from anyone else. If we evaluate this evidence according to the standard of reasonable doubt, we can be absolutely sure that Tolimir at that time knew absolutely nothing about the prisoners of war. The Trial Chamber concludes that Tolimir, when he found out, and we believe that Tolimir knew absolutely nothing at the time about POWs, was able to take adequate measures, that he was able to issue, for instance, appropriate instructions to his subordinate units. Well, one instruction was issued, it's D49, whereby Tolimir conveys an order from Karadzic regarding the attack on Srebrenica and which states: "Treat the civilian population and POWs in accordance with the Geneva Conventions of 12 July, 1949." Could Tolimir be satisfied that military officers would comply with an order from the Supreme Commander and their military duties? We believe so. Is this an instruction issued to someone who was known for respect for the duty to protect POWs for specific laws and regulations dealing with POWs, Exhibit D49, who on 12 July says that all the able-bodied military-aged men in Potocari need to be listed and registered? Was such a person informed that crimes were being committed? The Trial Chamber seems to have proceeded from the supposition that when somebody in the army issued an unlawful order, it is executed in a military way according to the normal hierarchy and the standard procedures in the army. The Army of Republika Srpska was not an army that was based on obedience but on duty, and the duty of the officers was to refuse an unlawful order. Considering that a criminal act was being committed, would somebody who was known to wish to protect POWs be informed that harm was going to be done to these prisoners? Of course we stand by all the legal grounds of appeal that we cited. I believe that I have already answered the question number 4 of the Appeals Chamber, whether the only reasonable conclusion for the Trial Chamber was that Tolimir intended to participate and significantly contributed to the JCE of killings. We believe that he did not participate, and since he did not participate he did not intend it, nor was he able to significantly contribute to the killing of prisoners from Srebrenica and he knew nothing about it. As for question number 5 of the Appeals Chamber, concerning ground of appeal 16 - that is to say, can Tolimir be considered responsible for his role in the killings in Srebrenica based on some other mode of liability apart from participation in the JCE? It is true that the indictment charges Tolimir according to Article 7(1) of the Statute. We believe that the Appeals Chamber should and has the right to consider whether the accused is culpable under some other mode of liability, but I wish to emphasise that the indictment was conceived under a mode of liability based on joint criminal enterprise and it is difficult to reconsider it now. Since the Defence asserts that in the relevant period Tolimir did not know about the murder operation and he did not contribute to it and did not participate in it nor did he intend to participate, therefore we believe that there is no reason whatsoever to charge Tolimir under any other mode of liability. Of course in any case the Appeals Chamber is at liberty, if they deem necessary, to instruct the parties to make their written submissions concerning alternative modes of liability within any time-limit they determine, and perhaps the appropriate time for that is only at the end of these appeals proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, this may be a question of interpretation, but I would want this to be quite precise. I read from the transcript: "I wish to emphasise that the indictment was conceived under a mode of liability based on joint criminal enterprise and it is difficult to reconsider it now." Now the indictment, as you point out, charge all modes of liability under 7(1) of the Statute including aiding and abetting under it, so it did not just charge one thing. Not just joint criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not manage to read the whole transcript, but I did emphasise all that. I said that Tolimir was charged with all modes of liability envisaged under 7(1) of the Statute, but the indictment itself was modelled and written in such a way that it deals exclusively with this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And of course it would be perhaps more appropriate for the Defence to respond in its reply if the Prosecution makes any submissions about alternative modes of liability such as aiding and abetting or something else. The next question, question number 6 of the Appeals Chamber, regards appeal ground number 21: Can Tolimir be convicted of genocide for participation in JCE of forcible removal if the Appeals Chamber should accept appeal ground 16? If the Appeals Chamber accepts the ground of appeal number 16 - that is, if it finds that the majority of the Trial Chamber erred in finding that the Tolimir was a participant in JCE of killings and that he significantly contributed to this JCE - then the conviction for genocide also falls away. In its ground of appeal 15, the Defence presented arguments to corroborate its assertion that Tolimir was not a participant of the JCE of forcible removal and that he did not contribute to the JCE of forcible removal of Srebrenica and Zepa populations. However if the Appeals Chamber decides differently, the participation in the JCE of forcible removal cannot be a sufficient foundation for conviction for genocide considering that the killings of Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica were the predominant factor in establishing both the genocidal intent and the qualification of forcible removal as an act of genocide. I will recall here the conclusions and the findings of the Appeals Chamber in Prosecutor versus Blagojevic and Jokic and Prosecutor versus Krstic in which the Trial Chamber has provided almost identical reasoning as the majority of the Trial Chamber in Tolimir. As the Appeals Chamber emphasised in Blagojevic and Jokic, paragraph 123, the reasoning of the Trial Chamber did not convince the Appeals Chamber that the operation of forcible removal in and of itself or together with killings and mistreatment in Bratunac is sufficient to demonstrate the intent of the principal participants, principal perpetrators, to destroy the protected group. In the appeals judgement in Krstic, in paragraph 35, it is clearly noted that forcible removal in and of itself does not constitute genocide. As a relevant fact, it is only a part of the entire factual evaluation. The conclusions of the Trial Chamber on the genocidal intent and the acts of genocide are founded primarily and almost exclusively on the consequences of the murder operation of Bosnian Muslims who were separated at Potocari or captured from the column that was breaking through towards Tuzla, which is clearly seen from paragraph 753 to 757 of the judgement. Therefore, should the Appeals Chamber accept the ground for appeal number 16, that there is no intent for genocide or JCE for genocide, Tolimir should be acquitted on Counts 1 and 2 of the indictment. And finally we come to a very problematic document. We are talking about Exhibit P488. The Defence has identified a lot of mistakes with regard to this document. There are a lot of translation mistakes because it contains certain things that are not seen in the original. Could you please bear with me for a moment. First of all, the majority of the Trial Chamber members have established that the document 488 is relevant to show the accused's mens rea during the operation in Zepa and that he was completely aware of the dire straits faced by the vulnerable population there. We are talking about paragraph 171 and that it shows intention to remove the population from Zepa as a contribution to the JCE of forcible transfer. Bearing in mind that context within which the report was sent by the accused as well as his -- its wrong meaning in paragraph 1091, and it shows the determination on behalf of Tolimir to destroy the population of Zepa. We believe that this conclusion on the part of the Trial Chamber is absolutely out of order. First of all, I have to provide an alternative argument. If this document is properly understood there is one explanation, and second argument would be provided if the Appeals Chamber does not accept the true contents of the document. I'll start with last things first. If the Appeals Chamber does not take into account what has been said about the document in the appeals proceedings, the unique position, the jurisprudence of the Tribunal is that when the Prosecution tries to prove the mens rea of the accused through inference, this should be done only on all the adduced evidence. When it comes to P488, the Trial Chamber erred in many respects which are pointed out in the grounds for appeal number 15. However, if we are looking at this document only to answer the question whether there was a genocidal intention, the document and the relevant context show that it was done only to achieve a certain military goal and nothing else, and that was to speed up the surrender of the Zepa Brigade. It was not an objective to destroy the Bosnian Muslim population in Zepa or part thereof as such. A majority of the Trial Chamber members arrived at the conclusion that this proposal was the ultimate measure, as a matter of fact, and that it had to be regard within the context of the goal which was the surrender of Muslims. This document, if it is understood in the way it was interpreted by the Trial Chamber, stands below the threshold of the genocidal intent because a genocidal intent implies a destruction of a certain group as a separate entity. This document does not show that the opinion was provided because of the destruction of the population, nor that the population was the primary target of all the activities. It doesn't demonstrate, contrary to what was concluded by the Trial Chamber, Tolimir's decisiveness and determination to destroy the population of Zepa as such. The Trial Chamber relied on the translation of this document. In this document, the most disputable word is probably the word "zbeg." The Trial Chamber considered the arguments provided by the accused during trial and in his closing argument, but it did not give up on the official translation. The word "zbeg" does not mean "refugees" or "displaced persons." The word "fleeing" cannot be found in the original. Tolimir did not suggest that refugees fleeing from something should be destroyed. His proposal was to destroy empty locations for which it had been established that potentially they represented places where Muslim populations could arrive at. I am referring to paragraph 79 of Judge Nyambe's dissenting opinion. Looking at the totality of events in Zepa, there is a conspicuous absence on any focus on any destruction of the civilian population. In addition to that, the Trial Chamber did not take into consideration the circumstances that the proposal, even if it had been tabled, could not have been implemented. Savcic, who during the relevant period of time was in Zepa, showed that locations that are mentioned in the documents were absolutely beyond the target of the Army of Republika Srpska. He described in very much detail the area, the terrain, and the circumstances that prevailed there. I would like to refer to Savcic's testimony recorded on transcript pages 15196 through 15197. This interpretation on the part of the Trial Chamber and that I have just quoted, that Tolimir did not suggest the destruction of the Muslim population, can be seen from the context itself. It says in this document that the Muslims were targeting and shooting at the UNPROFOR base in order to provoke a NATO reaction. They were in the process of transferring the population. And the document also says that the contactual group was expected to meet on the 25th of July, 1995. In such a situation, it would have been beyond any reason to propose destruction of the civilian population. However, a reasonable military measure in such a case was and would have been to destroy certain natural locations, not to destroy them as a matter of fact but to disable them in order to prevent the civilian population of going there so that the BiH Army would be forced to surrender as quickly as possible. According to the position of the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti has a question, so let me interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Gajic. About this translation issue. I worked yesterday on Exhibit P488, and this is not the only document where there were translation issues that could lead to different interpretations. Exhibit P488 is made up of four paragraphs, and in the first paragraph it is said that it would be better to directly negotiate after having caused human losses to the enemy forces. So this document refers to enemy forces, and you were right when you raised the translation issue for the word "zbegovi," where in Exhibit P488 in the English version it says "refugees," whereas in the French translation, because I requested the French translation for the B/C/S original document, it talks about a group of Muslim inhabitants fleeing. And if you want to interpret inhabitants, you can think about civilians. But I see no reference to the Muslim inhabitants. So I'm wondering whether the reason for that is that those Muslims came from three municipalities: Stublici, Radava, and Brloska Planina. Given your knowledge of the case, these people fleeing, were they civilians or military forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, we are talking about certain additions and mistakes in translations. And this is obvious. Translations cannot be uniform. I'll try to paraphrase this document. This is not about those who were fleeing from Stublici, Radava, and Brloska Planina. This is about destruction of "zbegovi" from those directions. This is about destruction of "zbegovi" from those directions. If in the Serbian version for a moment we ignore the words "'zbegovi' of the Muslim population," this is what I am reading: "We are of the opinion that destruction from the directions of Stublici...," and so on and so forth, "... Muslims would be forced to surrender more quickly." The word "fleeing" is not mentioned in the original document at all. It is simply an addition, a mere surplus in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence is open to any questions from the Judges of the Appeals Chamber in view of the fact that we have only a few minutes left. This is to say that I don't want to raise any other issues at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will ask my distinguished colleagues whether they have any questions. I see none. We still have about ten minutes. Mr. Kremer, to make your lunch time a bit more interesting today, I suggest that you reflect on the following question for when you make your presentation. I would like to refer, and you probably will not be surprised by this, to the Popovic case. In the Popovic case -- the trial. Of course, I'm not speaking of the appeal but of the trial. The trial rejected the charge that the forcible transfer of the women and children from Srebrenica and the Bosnian Muslims from Zepa fell within the ambit of Article 4(2)(C) of the Statute. That's Popovic trial judgement, paragraphs 849 and 854. The Popovic Trial Chamber specifically rejected the notion that the destruction of the social structure of the community and the inability of those who were forcibly transferred to reconstruct their lives - I'm skipping a few words - are the kinds of conditions intended to be prohibited by Article 4(2)(C) of the Statute. That's paragraph 854 of the trial judgement. This specific finding of the Popovic trial judgement was not challenged on appeal by the Prosecution. And my question to you is this: In your view, was the interpretation of Article 4 of the Statute in the Popovic case correct? Should the Appeals Chamber find that reasoning persuasive, even if not technically binding, authority for purposes of the present case, in the case of Tolimir, and of course 4(2)(C) as you know so well deals with genocide, and 4(2)(C) reads: "Deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part." So if you could, when you make your statement, please enlighten us on that -- on that -- on the relevance or not and the influence or not of this statement in Popovic. It probably does not make sense for me to ask you to use the five minutes before the break, so we will break now. And let me see how much time do we need now. I suppose that was 90 minutes. Ninety minutes. So in 90 minutes we will meet here, 90 minutes sharp counting from 12.15. We will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. The Appeals Chamber will now hear the Prosecution's response for two hours. I invite counsel for the Prosecution to present the Prosecution's submissions. Mr. Kremer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, let me first begin by answering the question posed by President Meron immediately before the break concerning the finding at the Popovic trial judgement in paragraph 854, that the forcible transfer operation was not found to be a condition deliberately imposed to bring about the physical destruction of the group. As a preliminary matter, let me note that the Prosecution's failure to appeal that point should not be viewed as accepting that finding. The Prosecution could not have appealed the conclusion in the Popovic case because there would have been no impact on the case since the Popovic Trial Chamber had found that the underlying acts of genocide, the killings, and serious bodily or mental harm were committed, and it determined that the accused acted with genocidal intent. But to get at the heart of your question, the difference between the findings by the Popovic and Tolimir Trial Chambers is explained by the fact that the two cases were charged differently. In the Popovic case, the Prosecution at paragraph 33 of the indictment charged the forcible transfer as the relevant condition of life alone. In this case, however, the Prosecution charged that it was the combined effect of the forcible transfer and the murder operation or the killing operation that consisted of the condition relevant under Article 4(2)(C) and that's our amended indictment at paragraph 24; thus, in the Popovic trial judgement, the Trial Chamber only focused on the forcible transfer operation - and you can see that at paragraph 854 of its judgement - where the Trial Chamber emphasised that: "The Trial Chamber notes that the Prosecution's allegation does not include the effect of the killings on the Bosnian Muslim social structure." In this case the Trial Chamber looked at "the combined effect of these operations" and how it had a "devastating effect on the physical survival of the Bosnian Muslim population in eastern Bosnia." And that's at paragraph 766. And our position is that the finding was entirely reasonable for the reasons put forward by the Trial Chamber in the judgement. And I hope that answers your question. Thank you. Let me now begin by giving a road map of our submissions, and our submissions basically will answer the seven questions and I -- I'm not optimistic there is any further time to elaborate on the issues because Mr. Gajic, too, has addressed only the seven questions. Just in terms of presentation, I will answer questions 1 through 4 and 6 and 7, Mr. Wood will answer question 5. The questions posed in your October 31st addendum go fundamentally to three issues: One, Tolimir's responsibility for the crimes as part of the JCE to murder; two, Tolimir's genocidal intent; and three, the crimes committed in Zepa. I will begin by discussing Tolimir's participation in the JCE to murder and explain why it was entirely reasonable for the Trial Chamber to find that Tolimir intended to participate in and significantly contributed to the JCE to murder. In that discussion, I will also explain why it was appropriate and necessary for the Trial Chamber to view Tolimir's acts, conduct, and knowledge in light of his position and role as the chief of the sector for intelligence and security affairs of the Army of Republika Srpska, the VRS. And when I complete my submissions, I hope to have fully answered questions 3 and 4. I will then discuss why the Chamber's finding, that Tolimir possessed genocidal intent, was reasonable. In doing so, I will explain that the Chamber properly looked at Exhibit P488 as one piece of evidence for assessing Tolimir's intent, and, in doing so, I will address both question 6 and 7. And, finally, I will address questions 1 and 2 on how the killings and serious bodily or mental harm committed in the Zepa operations were properly classified as underlying acts of genocide, and how and when the Bosnian Serb forces killed the leaders from Zepa it was properly determined that it was with genocidal intent. As the jurisprudence of the Tribunal recognises, the task of hearing, assessing, and weighing the evidence presented at trial is left primarily to the Trial Chamber. And I don't have to refer you but I will refer you to the recent Sainovic appeal judgement at paragraph 23 and the Kupreskic appeal judgement at paragraph 30. And because this assignment of this important judicial function to Trial Chambers, the Appeals Chamber gives a significant margin of deference to the findings of fact reached by a Trial Chamber. Only where the evidence relied on by the Trial Chamber could not have been accepted by a reasonable tribunal of fact or trier of fact or where the evaluation of the evidence is wholly erroneous does the Appeals Chamber substitute its own finding for that of the Trial Chamber. And that's again from Kupreskic appeal judgement at paragraph 30. I remind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I just ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] whether the significance is your own authority. Shall I repeat myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was inquiring whether the word "significant" which you have used to describe the margin of deference is your own description of whether it is taken from any -- in any case law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I would have to go back to the case law to see if the word is used, but having regard to the -- the history of judicial review in this -- appellate review in the Appeals Chamber there is, I would submit, a history or a practice of giving significant deference to the findings of fact made by Trial Chambers, particularly given the length of the trials, the number of witnesses heard, the issues that are being heard in relation to the meaning of documents in -- in the context of the -- the conflict as a whole and the specific allegations made by the Prosecution specifically. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm more content with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the margin of deference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could I just draw the attention of the Bench and the others in the room that the question asked by my colleague Judge Robinson in the transcript has been attributed to Judge Sekule and I'm told that Judge Sekule does not want to claim Judge Robinson's laurels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SEKULE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you. And on that point in this case the Trial Chamber heard over 400 -- 242 days of trial, listened to the testimony of 183 Prosecution witnesses, 4 Defence witnesses, and received 2.962 Prosecution exhibits and 533 Defence exhibits. The Trial Chamber judgement, I would submit, provides an excellent example on how to properly evaluate evidence and apply the reasonable doubt standard. The judgement first sets out the general principles the Trial Chamber applied at paragraphs 30 to 35 and then it proceeded to apply them. The judgement with its carefully and fully articulated reasons, we submit, does not allow for judicial intervention. Now let me now turn to the questions concerning Tolimir's participation in the JCE to murder, beginning with question 3. And this question is important because it is also reflected as a repeating theme in Tolimir's appeal; namely, his suggestion that he was convicted on the position -- on the basis of the position he held, not on what he did. In fact, he was convicted on what he did based on the position he held. In short, our answer to your question is no. The question was whether the Trial Chamber erred in relying, inter alia, on Tolimir's position as chief of the sector for intelligence and security affairs and his professional control of subordinate security and intelligence organs in finding that Tolimir was: One, aware of his subordinate's involvement in the JCE to murder; and two, intended to participate in the JCE to murder. The Trial Chamber reasonably used General Tolimir's position and role as assistant commander to Mladic in the VRS Main Staff and chief of the sector for intelligence and security affairs and of his professional control of subordinate organs in the VRS in assessing his awareness of his subordinates' involvement, his intention to participate in the JCE to murder, and to properly interpret Tolimir's acts and omissions in the performance of his duties which facilitated the murder operation. As an initial matter, the Trial Chamber was correct to look at Tolimir's position when assessing his participation in the JCE to murder. The Appeals Chamber at paragraph 192 of the Kvocka appeal judgement has held that while a position of authority is not a material condition required under JCE theory, it is a relevant factor in determining the scope of the accused's participation in the common purpose. Therefore, as a legal matter, the Trial Chamber correctly and properly looked at Tolimir's position when assessing the other evidence showing his JCE participation. In fact, it would have been an error not to rely on this evidence. Now the significance of General Tolimir's position is evident when you understand who he was, what his duties, powers, and authorities were, how the chain of command in the VRS worked, and why this was important when assessing his conduct. To murder over 5700 Bosnian Muslim men and boys over the span of only four days while having forcibly displaced up to 30.000 Bosnian Muslim civilians from Srebrenica and approximately 4400 civilians from Zepa required planning and co-ordination within the VRS starting with the Main Staff. It also required clear command responsibilities, an operational communication system and an enforced efficient functioning reporting system from the ground up to the VRS Main Staff. Most important was that each JCE member and their tools in the VRS acted in accordance with the line of subordination and the principle of unity of command. And I refer you to judgement paragraphs 95, 1125, and 1165.
