And we know that Tolimir was the assistant commander to Mladic in the VRS Main Staff and he's chief of the sector for intelligence and security affairs from as early as mid-December 1992. That's in trial judgement paragraph 913. Through his position, Tolimir commanded his immediate subordinates Ljubisa Beara, chief of security, and Petar Salapura, chief of intelligence. And he controlled the work of subordinate security and intelligence organs. And that's at trial judgements paragraph 103 to 104. And, Your Honours, paragraphs 103 to 122 detail the functioning of the sector of intelligence and security affairs based on the evidence that the Trial Chamber heard. Tolimir's professional control of his subordinate security and intelligence organs work was highly relevant because such a significant number of subordinates in his professional chain of command were involved in the murder operation and played a significant role in its success. They included Beara, Salapura, Radoslav Jankovic, Popovic, Kosoric, Golic, Momir Nikolic, Drago Nikolic, Trbic, Carkic, and military police among others. And that's found at trial judgement 1098. As General Skrbic told the Trial Chamber, VRS Main Staff assistant commanders were "experts for the implementation of the commander's orders and decisions in the best possible way." That's cited at trial judgement paragraph 916. As a VRS Main Staff assistant commander, General Tolimir was directly subordinated to Mladic. That's trial judgement paragraphs 92 and 914. He was responsible for implementing and monitoring all security and intelligence related orders from Mladic and was duty-bound to see that they were carried out. Tolimir was Mladic's order implementer, trial paragraph 916. General Tolimir was also the highest-ranking officer in the VRS with expertise in all prisoner-related matters including management of their detention, security, transportation, interrogation, and exchange. And that's found in trial judgement paragraphs 106, 110 to 111, 914, 916, and 920. And given his prisoner management function, as will be discussed later in more detail, he failed to fulfil one of his primary duties: To protect the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Do tell me, Mr. Kremer, if supposing for a moment that you would have had no evidence regarding Mr. Tolimir and Tolimir had anything to do with the POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You would only have his role which you explained. On the basis of his role and command responsibility, could you have made the same case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Even without any specific evidence about his involvement with the POWs? Just because we heard he was deputy number two and he had the role of intelligence security responsibilities --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: That brings me to my next point. You may have been divining what I'm about to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So I should just wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: What I'm about to say. Tolimir's other important function, and this, I think, is to Your Honour's question, was to prevent leaks of highly classified information as well as to cover up VRS actions and intentions which he did during the murder operations. He was the VRS secret keeper and intelligence gatherer. And that's found in trial judgements 914 to 915.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So you are saying now that there were certain actually evidentiary things bearing on the question of connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: My question was if you would not have had that latter evidence, just on the basis of his authority, could you say that it's inconceivable that as number two of Mladic you would not have known, et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: If -- if the only evidence you had that he was the number two person for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: -- General Mladic and nothing else --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: -- no other evidence, no orders, no activity, then obviously we wouldn't be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: But we have a pile of evidence that the Trial Chamber chronicled carefully and fully from people within the military, outsiders, and victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So it's not just the function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Not just the function at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: In fact, it's the function that gives meaning to what's happening. And a document by itself may have no special significance, but once you understand who is sending the document, who is receiving, and in light of what's going on in the ground, then it makes a lot more sense. And so it's -- his function gives context, gives meaning to the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kremer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And in addition to these key responsibilities, Tolimir had a very close relationship with Mladic and was described, as Mr. Gajic said earlier, his right-hand man, his eyes and ears, and the person Mladic trusted most. Mladic regularly consulted him before taking a decision, they worked closely together through the murder operation, and at a new year's celebration in January 1996, Mladic himself referred to Tolimir as being a part of his inner core that took the most important decisions during the war. And that's at trial paragraph 915 and 921. Mr. Gajic's suggestion that Krstic, who had just been appointed to the Drina Corps command at this time or at the time the killings were started, was similarly situated to Tolimir is not grounded in reality. Krstic was not in Mladic's inner core. Krstic was not a VRS Main Staff assistant commander responsible for implementing Mladic's decisions or due to Tolimir's specific expertise the highest-ranking officer for secret keeping and managing prisoners. Let me turn to the JCE to murder, which embraces question 4. Question 4 asks whether the Trial Chamber erred in finding that the only reasonable inferences from the evidence on the record were that Tolimir intended to participate in and significantly contributed to the JCE to murder. Our answer is no. The question, I would suggest, as framed misreads the judgement. In deciding on the essential elements of his criminal responsibility for JCE to murder, the Trial Chamber applied the law to the facts correctly. It concluded that Tolimir's significant contribution to and participation in the JCE to murder had been proved beyond reasonable doubt. And I refer you to trial judgement 1115 and 1129 which are the conclusions as to the significant contribution and shared intent. In making its factual decisions within paragraphs 1099 to 1128 where it discusses the supporting evidence to or the supporting findings for its conclusion, it made determinations on circumstantial evidence. And when it did so, it applied the only reasonable inference test. Where there was direct evidence or a combination of direct and circumstantial evidence, the Trial Chamber made its finding using the reasonable doubt standard. And this can be seen in several places in paragraphs 1099 to 1028. Our position quite simply is that the question, properly framed, would have been whether the Trial Chamber erred in finding that it had been established beyond reasonable doubt from the evidence on the record that Tolimir intended as opposed to that the only reasonable inferences from the record. Our position is that the only reasonable inference test is not the test for determining guilt or innocence or the essential elements of the crime. Now as I have mentioned, the Chamber took a comprehensive contextual approach when judging Tolimir's participation in and contribution to the murder. Today Mr. Gajic continued the Defence approach of referring to pieces of evidence in isolation. In contrast, the Chamber's conclusions were based on multiple strands of interconnecting and mutually corroborating evidence taken in context of all of the relevant evidence including, as we have just discussed, the evidence of Tolimir's position and responsibilities as well as his professional control over subordinate organs. Now, Mr. Gajic went through a chronology of events and challenged little pieces based on his interpretation which is similar to what he does in his appeal brief. I'm just going to highlight a few of the key events that the Trial Chamber relied on in making its decision about the individual criminal responsibility of General Tolimir in the JCE to murder. By the morning of 12 July, the Chamber found that a common plan existed among members of the Bosnian Serb forces to murder Bosnian Muslim able-bodied men from Srebrenica. And on the morning of the 12th, Tolimir's subordinates, Popovic, Momir Nikolic, and Kosoric, discussed the murder operation in front of Hotel Fontana. Mladic mirrored their discussions, remarking that morning in the Hotel Fontana meeting that his forces would screen the Bosnian Muslim men to identify war criminals and that the Bosnian Muslims could "survive or disappear." We know from what ensued that no actual registration or screening took place following the separation and capture of the Bosnian Muslim men and boys. On the contrary, as foreshadowed by Mladic, the men and boys were disappeared in the ensuing mass executions while the 30.000 women, children, and elderly were expelled from Srebrenica and were effectively disappeared from eastern Bosnia. Trial judgements 1045 to 1047. On the morning of the 12th, Tolimir was in Bijeljina issuing instructions to Todorovic, the chief of security of the Eastern Bosnian Corps to prepare the Batkovic collection centre for the arrival of 1.000 to 1300 POWs. It's at trial judgement 931. The POWs in question were the Bosnian Muslim men and boys who had gathered at Potocari following the Srebrenica attack and take-over and were being separated and detained by the Bosnian Serb forces, trial judgement 293. Throughout the day, Tolimir was receiving reports from his Drina Corps security and intelligence chiefs, Popovic and Golic, and others about the situation in Potocari. For instance, Tolimir received Popovic's late afternoon report stating that: "We are separating men from 17 to 60 years of age and we are not transporting them. The security organs and the state security are working with them." And that's trial judgement 1100, Exhibit P2069. Radoslav Jankovic, Tolimir's subordinate in the Main Staff intelligence administration, attended meetings at the Hotel Fontana on the 11th and 12th of July. The Trial Chamber had no doubt that Tolimir was informed of the discussions at these meetings, paragraph 1087. The Chamber found that Tolimir was made aware of the situation that transpired on the ground in Srebrenica, and that's in judgement paragraph 1100 to 1101. And Tolimir, by issuing two reports concerning the separations of the able-bodied Muslim men in Potocari as well as the arrests from the column himself, demonstrated his understanding of what was happening in Potocari. And that's judgement paragraph 1101, and the two reports are P2203 and D64. Now what happens on the next day, July 13th, is critical to an understanding of why General Tolimir was properly convicted. On the 13th of July, Tolimir's communications completely changed, and this change becomes highly relevant particularly when viewing what Tolimir did and said in relation to what was happening on the ground. By the early afternoon of 13 July, approximately 5.000 Bosnian Muslim males from the column that had fled Srebrenica had been captured by or had surrendered to Bosnian Serb forces. That's in trial judgement paragraphs 315 to 321, 323, 330, 336, and 820. Between 2.00 to 3.00 p.m., noting that over 1.000 Bosnian Muslims were being detained in the Novo Kasaba area, Tolimir proposed measures to the MP battalion commander Malinic to "take measures to remove war prisoners from the main Milici-Zvornik road. Place them somewhere indoors or in an area protected from observation from the ground or the air," judgement paragraph 936 and 1103, and Exhibit P125. To clarify, it was along the Milici-Zvornik and the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac roads where the Bosnian Muslim males from the column were being captured or were surrendering. Also, the only forces who could observe the prisoners from the air, the only forces with access to air-space above the area were the internationals. Tolimir's proposal was incorporated into Mladic's order issued that same night regarding control of information about prisoners and prohibition of traffic. And the Chamber found that both reflected the effort to conceal the murder operation and both were acted upon, trial judgement 946, 1055, and 1103. Now between the issuance of Tolimir's proposal and Mladic's subsequent order, up to 1.000 prisoners in this area were taken to the Kravica warehouse and were executed. The thousands of other prisoners were placed on buses, in schools, and in hangars in Bratunac to spend the night hidden from sight, being moved to mass execution sites in the Zvornik area of responsibility in the coming days. And that's at judgement paragraphs 946, 1053, footnote 4148, and 1054. The Chamber reasonably concluded that General Tolimir's proposed measures "reflect the co-ordinated effort to conceal the despicable plan contemplated among the members of the JCE to murder," judgement paragraph 1103. But it isn't these actions alone that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: My colleague Judge Guney would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. I understand that the operation conducted in Zepa and Srebrenica had different features. However, it is my understanding that they both aimed at the removing the Bosnian Muslim civilian population within the area whether by forcible displacement or killings or both. Would this be also a reasonable assessment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The answer to your question is yes. The Trial Chamber looked at the operation singly because the operation initially, starting with Directive 7, Krivaja 95, orders, and looking at the forces involved, the nature of the attacks, there were similarities. The one single difference between Srebrenica and Zepa was the fact that the Zepa men, the soldiers, were able to escape into the forests before they could be captured. And that -- whereas able-bodied men and boys were captured in Srebrenica and ultimately captured as the column was attempting to flee, and we'll get into this later, but our position is, and the Trial Chamber rightly found, that the operation was a single operation against the three enclaves, Gorazde, Srebrenica, and Zepa. We're just dealing with Srebrenica and Zepa. And the Srebrenica enclave being the biggest was attacked first, Zepa being nearby was attacked by the same forces, and we agree with your question that although there are slight differences the -- it was based on both a forcible transfer a -- a military attack to transfer the population out. It turned into a JCE to murder at some point, and the Zepa situation didn't turn into the scale of murders simply because the targets -- the military-aged men had fled to the forests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could you expand a little bit on the last point you have made. How do you explain that there were no mass killings in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: By the time they took the town, there were no military-aged men left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So that's basically it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Nobody to kill?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: That's my understanding. They could have pursued -- it was pursued and they finally fled to Serbia and other parts, but the people left in Zepa were primarily women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The Chamber -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If I may keep you for another moment. With regards to the involvement of General Tolimir that you have been talking about, is the joint criminal enterprise to murder the only mode of liability that fits these factual descriptions? Would other modes fit them; in particular, aiding and abetting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Mr. Wood will answer that question. The answer is other modes would fit. Our position is that the JCE to murder is the most appropriate under the circumstances of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: In contrast to Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: In contrast to Krstic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Getting back to -- there are two additional actions by Tolimir on the 13th with -- which reinforce the conclusion that he was involved in the JCE to murder. First, that evening Tolimir sent a telegram to the VRS Main Staff and to Gvero personally proposing the transfer of 800 prisoners to Sjemec farm to be "done at night." At a time when all facilities in Bratunac were already overloaded with prisoners, and that's found in judgement paragraphs 1105 to 1106, this proposal was consistent with his earlier proposal to detain the Bosnian Muslims prisoners indoors and out of sight from the ground and air. And that's again found in P125.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Can you explain for the record what you mean by "to be done at night"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Under cover of darkness where you couldn't be seen by either the aerial surveillance by the internationals or seen clearly by other people who might be providing information, sources of information to the internationals. The whole point of the exercise was to keep the operation secret so they could complete it, and we have to recognise that before the murders started they were digging graves in order to bury the bodies and cover them up and we have more evidence at the end after the operation is over of the reburials in order to keep this from being disclosed as the heinous crime that it was ultimately shown to be. In addition to carrying out his secret keeping duties, in other words, concealing the murder operation, he was also actively contributing to it through his prisoner management and duties and capabilities. He was well aware that Sjemec was not an appropriate facility to house prisoners in. He knew that there was no agricultural work to be done there and that like the Kravica warehouse the fate of any prisoners taken there would be certain death at the hands of the VRS. Tolimir's Sjemec telegram was sent around the time when Tolimir's subordinates, Beara, Momir Nikolic, and Drago Nikolic, were working out the practical details of the killing operation including arranging for the burial of hundreds of Muslim men killed at the Kravica warehouse that afternoon and evening as well as organising the transfer of the Bosnian Muslim prisoners from Bratunac to Zvornik where they would be killed. And I refer you to judgement paragraphs 364 to 366, 402 to 404, 1055 to 1057. Second additional point. As early as 13 July, Tolimir cancelled his previous order to Todorovic to prepare Batkovic for a thousand to 1300 prisoners. He told Todorovic: "Drop any further preparations. The task has been abandoned." Todorovic explained this meant nothing "would come out of it. The prisoners would not be coming." And the judgement paragraphs 555, 951, 1103, and paragraph -- or transcript paragraph 12942. Your Honours, when Tolimir instructed that preparation should cease, he as the highest-ranking officer involving prisoner management knew the prisoners were to be murdered. Importantly, on 13 July, Tolimir's direct subordinate Beara was already in Bratunac arranging the murder of prisoners. And that's in judgement paragraphs 364 to 366 and 1055. Given Tolimir's professional command and control over Beara, he knew both of Beara's whereabouts and specific tasks. And this becomes abundantly clear in light of what Tolimir says and does in subsequent days. Viewed together, the Chamber's conclusion that Tolimir knew of the murder plan by the afternoon of 13 July was entirely reasonable. And I refer you to that conclusion at paragraph 1104. Turning now to the 14th of July, Tolimir continued to take steps to conceal the murder operation and his direct subordinates continued to be active in it. General Tolimir conveyed a warning to Mladic -- from Mladic to the Drina Corps command and subordinate units, including the Zvornik Brigade, concerning the presence of unmanned aircraft, judgement paragraph 1108. At this time the transportation of the remaining prisoners from Bratunac into the Zvornik area and the killings of up to 2500 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were taking place at Orahovac in the Zvornik area of responsibility. Also ongoing were the final executions at Kravica as well as the transportation to the Glogova burial site of up to 1.000 bodies of Bosnian Muslim men who had been killed at Kravica warehouse the previous day. And that's judgement paragraphs 353 to 371 and 376 as well as 405 to 439. Tolimir's warning supports his knowledge of what was happening to the thousands of men who had been captured on the 12th and 13th of July. As the Trial Chamber reasonably found in the last sentence of paragraph 1108: "Given that on this day the killings in Zvornik started at Orahovac, the only reasonable inference is that the accused sent the warning in order that the murder operation would be carried out without being detected." Tolimir's proposal to shoot down the aircraft also reflects the measures he was willing to take as part of his secret keeping function. The next day on the 15th of July, killings continued in the Petkovci dam, Rocevic school, and Kozluk. These killings, like the previous days killings in Orahovac and the Petkovci school, were carried out by the Zvornik Brigade military police under the supervision of Tolimir's subordinate security organs including Popovic and Drago Nikolic, judgement paragraphs 417 to 418, 442, 460 to 471, 481 to 482, 1059 to 1060. Throughout this time Beara was not just supervising the detention sites but was intimately involved with obtaining troops to ensure the ruthlessly efficient continuation of the mass executions of the Bosnian Muslim men and boys and he remained in close contact with Popovic. And that's judgement paragraphs 1058 to 1060. On the 16th of July Tolimir issued instructions to his subordinates in the intelligence administration, including Salapura, concerning safer ways to communicate to prevent detection. That same day the 10th Sabotage Detachment, a unit controlled by Salapura, was executing prisoners at the Branjevo military farm, judgement paragraphs 490 to 500, 508, 957, and 1109. In addition, Popovic was present in the area having requested 500 litres of fuel to be provided for the transportation of the prisoners from Kula school to the Branjevo farm. Judgement paragraph 1061, footnote 2156, Exhibit P846. The Chamber reasonably found that the accused as the direct superior of Salapura was kept abreast of all of the actions of the 10th Sabotage Detachment and it reasonably concluded that "it is inconceivable that the accused was kept in the dark about the murders in the relevant sites at the time. Instead, he tacitly approved to make these murders happen." Judgement paragraphs 115 to 118, 120 to 122 and 1112. The same evening on the 16th of July, Tolimir was at a meeting at the Main Staff headquarters with Mladic and others to plan the so-called sweep operations in the Bratunac area designed to eliminate any remaining Bosnian Muslim men who were fleeing and had not yet surrendered and been murdered. Tolimir stated that Beara was in the Drina Corps zone of responsibility, reflecting, again, that he knew of Beara's activities and whereabouts. At the time, the ongoing murder operation in the Zvornik area was coming to a close, judgement paragraph 958 to 959 and 1109. Evidence indicates that by the 18th of July rumours concerning the fate of the Bosnian Muslim males was beginning to circulate within the international community, paragraph 1062. On this day through his subordinate Jankovic, Tolimir was consulted on the fate of evacuation of workers from Medecins Sans Frontieres and their local staff who were highly visible and known to the international community. His advice was to let them go to divert the attention and pressure from the international community about the whereabouts of the Srebrenica men, judgement paragraph 1110. This shows that as part of his secret keeping function Tolimir attempted to cover up the murders even after they had been mostly completed and that he had authority to release prisoners. Tolimir's actions on the 22nd of July reinforce that he knew about the murder operation and was in constant contact with his subordinates involved in the executions. Tolimir spoke to his subordinate Popovic and instructed Popovic to "do his job." And, as we know, the next day Popovic supervised the 10th Sabotage Detachment in the Bisina killings. The Chamber reasonably concluded that he knew about these murders as well as the Branjevo farm murders carried out by the 10th Sabotage Detachment six days earlier, that he had tacitly approved to make them happen, and that he no doubt shared the intent to carry them out, judgement paragraphs 976, 1111, and 1112. But even after the murder operation was completed, Tolimir continued to exercise his secret keeping and prisoner management functions relating to the JCE to murder. Contrary to Mr. Gajic's statement about Tolimir's care for the proper treatment of prisoners, in late July and early August 1995 Tolimir issued instructions in conflict with military regulations and international law, that detainees not be registered and not be reported to international organisations, Exhibit P122 and Exhibit P2875. Looked at in conjunction with his orders throughout the murder operation to conceal the whereabouts of the Bosnian Muslim men who were being transported and executed, these instructions confirm his intention to keep the murder operation a secret, judgement paragraphs 671, 997, and 1123. In August and September 1995 when asked by family members of Bosnian Muslim men and boys who had just been executed en masse why POW exchanges weren't taking place, Tolimir deliberately lied explaining that only a small number of enemy soldiers had been captured, judgement paragraphs 1003 to 1004 and 1114. He knew, of course, that thousands upon thousands of men had been captured and executed in mid-July and that as of September and into October his subordinates were participating in reburial operations designed to conceal this genocide, judgement paragraphs 558 to 565, 1064, 1066, and 1114. Your Honours, in addition to these positive contributions to the murder operation, his intent, knowledge, and responsibility is enhanced by what he failed to do. The Trial Chamber was entirely reasonable in concluding that despite "his knowledge of the situation on the ground and of his obligations towards POWs, there is no evidence that Tolimir attempted to distance himself from the crimes and take any action to fulfil his duties towards POWs." And that's at judgement paragraph 1128. His failure to protect the Bosnian Muslim prisoners from Srebrenica significantly contributed to the JCE to murder, that's another quote from 1128, as is the following, Tolimir engaged himself in the covering up the common purpose of the JCE to murder and chose not to act resulting in the commission of crimes. To conclude in answer to your question 4, given all of the mutually reinforcing evidence on the record, taken as a whole, including the evidence of Tolimir's position and responsibilities, his professional control of his subordinates, his acts and omissions at the relevant time, what actually took place on the ground following the fall of Srebrenica, and the fact that vast numbers of his subordinates under his professional command and professional control were active participants in the murder, it was reasonable of the Trial Chamber to conclude that the -- that Tolimir intended to participate in and significantly concluded -- contributed to the JCE to murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Is there another alternative possible interpretation to the orders not to register?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: If you look at the order in isolation, maybe. If you looked at it in the context of what is happening -- what had happened and what was happening at the time, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: It's an obligation under the third Geneva Convention to register. I think it's quite clear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remind you that my remarks contain Tolimir's key acts and omissions from which the Chamber inferred that Tolimir was a member of and contributed to the JCE to murder. And I remind you that the Trial Chamber did not view any of the evidence in isolation. Each fact was viewed in context. And the Chamber's ultimate conclusion was based on the entire body of evidence, not just one exhibit. The Chamber's detailed and comprehensive analysis of these matters can be found at paragraphs 1099 to 1129 of the judgement. And as I've said, the conclusion as to Tolimir's criminal responsibility was made based on what was reasonable and should not be interfered with. And as you've asked and I've forecast, Mr. Wood will discuss the Chamber's question relating to the other modes of responsibility. Let me now move to Tolimir's genocidal intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] One second. I am looking at paragraph 650 and so on of the judgement regarding evacuation from Zepa. You mentioned in answering my questions a few minutes ago regarding why there were no large-scale killings in Zepa by saying that there were no militarily-aged men left. Paragraph 651: "The departure of military-aged men from Zepa and the interlinked issue of the intended POW exchange were also discussed and Torlak said that departure of military-aged men would be the biggest problem in the implementation,..." et cetera. So these militarily-aged men were not killed. How to reconcile that with the genocidal intent of Tolimir that you have argued?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'll deal with that shortly. But basically his intent can be looked at as a separate issue. We have to determine whether there were underlying acts of genocide and whether Tolimir had genocidal intent. The fact that these military-aged men were able to flee to the forest and hide and the VRS didn't have the capacity to pursue them, and the Trial Chamber also discussed the fact that it was becoming apparent very soon that the situation in Srebrenica was a grave one, and in fact people who had escaped Srebrenica were arriving in Zepa and giving the inhabitants information about what had happened to the -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I have a very good recollection that actually there was some evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I have a very good recollection that there was some actually arranged evacuation of those military-aged men from Zepa. Now, if they --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: There -- there is an order that I think Mr. Gajic referred to that -- a Serbian report that suggests that the ABiH ordered them to evacuate, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So in short, there were some military men --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- who -- and obviously there was no intent to kill them. It's not that there were no military-aged men as you answered before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: There were no military-aged men that were captured that could be killed. Whether the intent to kill them had they captured them is -- is a factual question that is a little bit complicated and I'll try and deal with it in the genocide part, giving you some context. And hopefully I can resolve your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Your uncertainty. And if I don't, I'll try to answer any further questions. Turning now to Tolimir's conviction for genocide and questions 6 and 7. The Trial Chamber properly found that Tolimir had genocidal intent and committed genocide, and this finding was based on a wide range of facts which the Chamber summarised in paragraph 1172 of the judgement. The Chamber relied on the fact that Tolimir was an active participant in both the forcible transfer and murder JCEs, and such evidence was highly relevant to its determination of Tolimir's genocidal intent because the Chamber found that the goal of these two operations went beyond the mere dissolution of the Bosnian Muslims of eastern Bosnia, found that "these operations were aimed at destroying this Bosnian Muslim community and preventing reconstruction or reconstitution of this group in the area," and that's judgement 766. And it thus found that both the forcible transfers and the murders were carried out with genocidal intent and that Tolimir knew this, and that's judgement paragraph 1166. The Chamber further relied on Prosecution Exhibit 488, Tolimir's July 21 proposal to destroy groups of fleeing Muslim refugees. And the Chamber found that this was a compelling example of Tolimir's own words demonstrating his genocidal intent. And I'll deal with question 7 first. Exhibit 488, which asks whether the Trial Chamber erred in relying on this exhibit to infer Tolimir's genocidal intent, our answer is, no, the Trial Chamber did not err. In fact, the Trial Chamber would have erred if it had not relied on this exhibit when inferring his genocidal intent. And let's just look at the document briefly and ask ourselves why. Quoting from the document, and this is the same passage that was referred to by Judge Antonetti earlier this morning, and I'm reading from the English translation, not the French, because I don't have it: "We believe that we could force Muslims to surrender sooner if we destroy groups of Muslim refugees fleeing from the direction of Stublic, Radava, and Brloska Planina." The fundamental question for genocidal intent is did Tolimir intend to destroy a part of the group as such, and it is hard to imagine evidence more relevant to genocidal intent than Tolimir's own words. The Trial Chamber reasonably found at paragraph 1171 of the judgement that the document "manifests the accused's determination to destroy the Bosnian Muslim population." And it noted in the paragraph in the exhibit that it showed Tolimir's state of mind during the forcible removal operation and his full knowledge of the predicament of the vulnerable civilian population in Zepa. And it also noted that the document showed his "fervent and tactical intention to remove the Bosnian population from the Zepa enclave." The Chamber also relied in this paragraph on the timing of the document. It was issued on the 21 July, 1995, after the Bosnian Muslim population had been forced out of Potocari, resulting in the serious bodily and mental harm and during the time-period when the accused was deeply involved in covering up the murder operation being carried out with genocidal intent and in preparing the forced movement of the Bosnian Muslim population of Zepa. And direct evidence like this of genocidal intent is rare as the Appeals Chamber recently noted in Karadzic 98 bis appeal judgement at paragraph 80. I just want to turn to Mr. Gajic's arguments today on P488. Mr. Gajic today wrongly focused on the term "surrender" at the beginning of the relevant paragraph and claims that P488 is only involved in a military objective. However, the Trial Chamber reasonably found that Tolimir's reference in paragraph 488 to "ABiH surrender" formed part of his overall goal of expelling the Bosnian Muslim population from Zepa, and I refer you to paragraph 1171 of the judgement. And this parallels the Chamber's finding that the attack on the two enclaves was directed at the civilian populations in the enclaves even if soldiers were present there, and that's in judgement paragraph 706. On the translation issue, which Mr. Gajic discussed this morning and discussed as well with Judge Antonetti, he repeats his trial arguments about the translation of P488, particularly the word "zbeg." The Trial Chamber specifically addressed these arguments and reasonably rejected them for two reasons: One, the Chamber properly relied on the official CLSS version of the document and this version translated the relevant phrase as "group of refugees." But perhaps more importantly and more significantly, the Chamber reasonably found that even if Tolimir's translation of "place of refuge" would be accepted, it would still find the intended targets were Bosnian Muslim civilians. This was because two witnesses, Ljubomir Obradovic, chief of operations in the VRS Main Staff, and Milomir Savcic, commander of the 65th Protection Regiment, both confirmed that Tolimir's proposal contained in P488 was aimed at fleeing civilians. And I refer you to paragraph 1091 and footnote 4290 of the judgement. Judge Nyambe in her dissent on this document, cited today by Mr. Gajic, did not address the evidence of these two witnesses who testified about P488 itself. She instead relied on a different witness who may have been talking about the word "zbeg" but did so in the context of a different document. And I refer you to transcript 8624 to 8626. And finally, Mr. Gajic today argued that the proposal to destroy the refugees could not be implemented. I would suggest that this suggests -- that this glosses over the importance that Tolimir was willing to even make such a radical proposal. That's what is important. Not whether it was possible to carry it out. I see the time is close to where we will take a break, I think. But perhaps I could be assisted by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes, you are assisted positively by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We agree. So we will now have a pause of 20 minutes and we will reconvene at 20 minutes past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Continue the response by the Prosecution. Mr. Kremer, you are continuing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Just continuing on from where I was, I'm -- given that Exhibit P488 is probative on its face, it is made even more compelling by the other evidence of Tolimir's genocidal intent. First example of this other evidence is his use of and encouragement of derogatory and dehumanising language. The Chamber found that he personally used derogatory terms such as "Turks" and "balijas" when discussing POW exchanges or negotiations with the ABiH, see judgement paragraph 1168. He also from his position as assistant commander condoned the use of these same terms by his subordinates, same paragraph. The Chamber concluded that Tolimir used and encouraged such language to promote "an attitude that Bosnian Muslims were human beings of a lesser value with a view to eradicate this particular group of the population from the eastern Bosnian Herzegovina," judgement paragraph 1169. Next example is Tolimir's awareness of the genocide; specifically, the Trial Chamber's finding that he knew that both the forcible transfer and the murder operations were being carried out with genocidal intent. I refer you to judgement paragraphs 1166 and 1172. In particular he was aware of the scale of the atrocities and the general context which the jurisprudence says can help show genocidal intent. That's the recent Karadzic 98 bis appeals judgement at paragraph 80. In terms of his awareness, I refer you to the Chamber's analysis, and I'm starting to shorten my submissions to give Mr. Wood an opportunity to address Your Honours on alternative modes, I refer you to paragraphs 1038, 1093, 1094, and 1109 of the judgement. But even assuming that P488 is not clear on its face, on the 21st of July, 1995, when he proposed to destroy Bosnian Muslim refugees, he was aware the genocide was in full swing and he was actively involved in the murder operation. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I'm looking at the transcript. With regards to the point you made that both the forcible transfer --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- and the murder operations were being carried out with a genocidal intent. Mr. Kremer, if I were to ask you to give me the strongest single piece of evidence on the genocidal intent for forcible transfer, let's leave genocide -- Srebrenica aside, just to help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I would say it's the document P488 taken in the context of the events at the time it's written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And again, what would be the sentence in it that you would consider the most persuasive?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I think it's the quote that we're discussing, that Judge Antonetti referred to, and confirmed by the two witnesses Obradovic and Savcic that they were talking about destroying fleeing civilians. And -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And if you're -- I'm sorry. My colleague advises me that the -- the context and also the evidence itself is that the forcible transfer operation had taken place in Potocari or took place in Potocari together with the murder operation, and I -- I was interpreting your question as Zepa alone, but if it's the forcible transfer globally, then it's the fact that the forcible transfer operation included Srebrenica, included Zepa, and took place in the context of the murder operation itself and that this particular document that is the subject matter of this question helps confirm his genocidal intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And if you were to, for analytical purposes to separate the two, you speak only of Zepa, genocidal intent with intent to transfer, what is the strongest piece that you could suggest to the Bench to reflect upon when it comes to deliberating on the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I would say that it's entirely artificial to split the baby. I don't think we come up with any wisdom like Solomon did in terms of solving the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But, of course, in previous cases on these complex issues, Krstic, Popovic, these issues were treated separately, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: It was a pleading -- they were treated separately because it was a pleading issue. In this particular case the indictment combined the two operations --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: -- into the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: -- support for the genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- ever in contrast to previous jurisprudence which combines the two. And analytically, I ask a legitimate question. Imagine that you'd just give me the strongest argument you have for genocidal intent on Zepa alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: That's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: This previous came out of the previous jurisprudence of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it has. This is the first case where Zepa -- the Zepa evidence has been fully integrated into a finding of genocide, and instead of looking at it contextually as a whole, I'm unfortunately being asked to look at this piece after -- without -- and ignore everything that went before, and it's the context of the entire operation. So Zepa taken as a forcible transfer, we have two acts - and I'll be candid - we have only two acts, underlying acts of genocide: We have the killing of the three leaders and we have the mental harm to the people who were transported out. Those are the two genocidal acts. The intent of Tolimir to commit genocide flows from his knowledge of everything that went before. He's involved -- he is on the ground involved in the forcible removal with negotiations, he knows the entire situation, he knows what's happened in Srebrenica, that 30.000-plus had been forcibly removed, that over 5700 men and boys had been killed, and all of that with this document, his derogatory words and everything else the Chamber referred to supports a finding of genocide. I think if you're looking for a genocide that it looks, smells, and tastes like genocide, it looks different than Srebrenica. There is no doubt about that. But in terms of the purely academic discussion, we have the underlying acts of genocide, we have the genocidal intent, and we have the supporting background knowledge of Tolimir from which you can infer his genocidal intent. But please don't view this as a concession that we agree that we should split the baby. We shouldn't. This case has to be looked at through the lens of the forcible transfer operation and the murder operation and evaluated as a whole and his genocidal intent determined as a -- at the end as to whether or not he intended -- he had the genocidal intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Suppose the Bench finds that the case has not been made out for treating both Zepa and Srebrenica as a whole, is it still open to the Bench to see whether the case is made out in respect of each separately?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Are we talking genocide or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBERTSON
utterances.text: Genocide, genocide. I am trying to really make a case for you to answer Judge Meron's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: No, I understand. I -- it depends on what basis that determination is made which will then form my answer. If the basis for finding that the murder operation, which is the -- which seems to be falling off on the questions asked by the Chamber, is not proven beyond a reasonable doubt, then the question is are all of the findings that the Trial Chamber made still there. And if they are all still there but the legal test has not been made, then our argument is that if you take all of those factual findings vis-à-vis the background, you can still support a conviction for genocide using his membership contributions to the JCE to forcibly transfer in light of the genocidal intent that he was aware of in the Bosnian Serb forces and the other members of the JCE in pursuing both the murder operation and so on. You don't have to be a member or criminally responsible for the other acts in order to have genocidal intent and make a contribution to the genocide, and there is no -- as long as the contribution is significant and made with the specific intent to destroy a whole -- the group in whole or in part, then that is enough. And what our simple answer is that they're looking at what is his contribution to the JCE to forcibly transfer and what did he know, and the Chamber found that when he was contributing to the forcible transfer, he was aware that the operation was being carried out with genocidal intent. And then the question becomes did he have personally genocidal intent, and they found he did for the reasons that the Chamber expressed based on this document and other evidence. So the -- your Question 6 causes us difficulty in terms of answering because it doesn't fully identify what the theoretical basis for the wiping away of the JCE to murder is. If it's based on all of ground 16 is allowed, each and every one of the 23 specific grounds, which is basically we're pretending that Srebrenica didn't happen and that General Tolimir had no role in it, then the answer is maybe we don't have a genocide in Zepa based on forcible transfer. But as I say, if it's only -- the proof isn't up to beyond a reasonable doubt, whether it's based on intent or whether it's based on the significance of his contributions, then that's another question because the Chamber does make an enormous amount of factual findings about the murder operations, about what he knew, about the genocidal intent of the members of the VRS who were carrying it out, and for all of the reasons that the Chamber articulate found that he had genocidal intent and was aware that the people perpetrating the crimes, the murder operation, even though he may not have been involved in it, were doing it with genocidal intent. So our position is in that circumstance you still end up sustaining the conviction for genocide but on a different basis than the Chamber articulated. But it's very difficult for me to answer the question with a lack of specificity because for -- if you -- because of the 23 grounds in -- ground of appeal 16 is 1 allowed, 2 allowed, 3 allowed, which -- what other permutations it becomes so complicated that it would take almost a book to answer the question depending what the -- what was possible. So my simple answer is, to the one, yes, it's possible. But again, if -- if we're going to be saying based on your best piece of evidence, that's almost an unfair question. There was a lot of evidence. Tell me what evidence the Chamber accepts that isn't problematical, and I can give you a well-reasoned explanation as to why there should be a conviction for genocide. But I -- sort of hypothetically it is unfair, I would say, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I realise we have been quite difficult on you, Mr. Kremer. Our object is to do our job of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: To get the best arguments possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: No, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm hoping to communicate how -- we've thought long and hard about this and it's been quite difficult, but we finally came to the answer that I've just given you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I think that my colleagues --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: We hope to be helpful but I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We've talked long about this question. I don't think we can elucidate it more. We will consider it very carefully when we sit down to deliberate it carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you so much and can you proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just trying to figure out where we should go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mind you to, you said to ask you to point out to the strongest single --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- piece of evidence on the basis of separation. I don't think that the question is unfair. It's typical in criminal cases that the judges would ask you this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: In a criminal case that is reasonably straight-forward, but here we have a decision that was entirely based on a single analysis of two JCEs and conceptualising only part of it and knowing, you know, as I say, it's fine to say, to look at it from the JCE to only to forcibly transfer but in what context. I need to know to answer the question in a way that helps you what part of evidence is left for the Chamber to consider. Is it all of the evidence of the murder or are we pretending that Srebrenica didn't exist or didn't happen. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We never suggested that today, did we?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting it. But that's -- that's the unwritten or unsaid premise. Turning to -- I'm going to move to the answer to question one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly give us a page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: You asked whether the operations in Zepa resulted in the commission of genocidal acts if viewed separately, I'll try to deal with it, from the killings in Srebrenica. By genocidal acts we understand that you are asking whether acts took place that constitute the actus reus of genocide, not whether the acts were committed with genocidal intent. In short our answer to the question as I've said is yes and the Trial Chamber reasonably found two categories of underlying acts of genocide committed by the Bosnian Serb forces during the Zepa operations killings and serious bodily or mental harm. As to the killings, at paragraph 751 to 752 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber concluded that the Bosnian Serb forces killed three of the most prominent Bosnian Muslim leaders in Zepa, Mehmed Hajric, Amir Imamovic, and Avdo Palic, and that these killings constituted the underlying genocidal act of killings members of the protective group under 4(2)(A) of the Statute. Remember that immediately after the take-over of Zepa all three leaders were arrested, held in detention, Hajric and Imamovic were beaten, and all three of them were violently murdered and buried in a mass grave near the prison where Hajric and Imamovic were last seen. That's in paragraph 658 to 680, 1152, and footnote 2867. And our position is that this is a reasonable finding based on the evidence. In terms of the serious bodily and mental harm of the displaced persons, the Chamber found that the Bosnian Muslims forcibly displaced from Zepa suffered serious mental harm, an underlying act of genocide, under 4(2)(B), and that's found in paragraphs 758 to 759 of the judgement. And recall that they made similar findings vis-à-vis the killings and the serious mental harm of the people in Zepa and Potocari. The -- or in Srebrenica and Potocari. In the case of Zepa, the Trial Chamber did a careful and detailed analysis of the combined effects caused by the entire Zepa operation on the Bosnian Muslim population and the comprehensive analysis is found through several sections, paragraph 600 to 653, 758 to 759, and 1028 to 1030. In the time that we have left, obviously it would be impossible to detail all the facts, so I'll just highlight a couple of them quickly, wanting to make sure that we have time for Mr. Wood. Beginning in early July and continuing to the 23rd of July, civilian centres in Zepa and surrounding villages were subjected to VRS armed incursions, artillery attacks, mortar fire, and heavy machine-gun fire. Numerous individuals, including children, were injured, and at least 30 homes were destroyed in the first few days of the attack, paragraph 600 to 1029. The psychological trauma caused by being subject to constant bombardment and the real possibility of being killed was compounded by several factors. One was that the Zepa population began to learn about the fate of the Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica, creating a state of panic that was intended by the VRS. There was a fear that the Bosnian Serb forces might enter Zepa and kill everyone including the women and children. I refer you to paragraph 603 and 1031 and footnote 2613. Tolimir played on this fear by linking the events of -- in Srebrenica with the fate of the Zepa population. On 13 July, during the very first meeting between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Muslim leaders, Tolimir drew parallels with Srebrenica informing the leaders Srebrenica has fallen and now it's Zepa's turn, judgement paragraph 607. During the attacks that followed, Tolimir took steps to enhance the psychological pressure on Zepa's population. He made arrangements for the delivery of loud speakers, and those loud speakers were used to broadcast Mladic's voice echoing throughout Zepa. And I refer you particularly to trial transcript 4821 and judgement paragraph 643 for the statement as to what Mladic was saying on the broadcast. On the 25th of July, exhausted and in a state of psychological distress, the Bosnian Muslim population, mostly women, children, and elderly went to the buses. As I said earlier, the able-bodied men from Zepa fled for their lives, especially as it became increasingly clear to the Bosnian Muslims from Zepa that the missing men from Srebrenica had been killed and they were fearful of being killed so they fled. Paragraph 674, footnote 2903. And those are just a few of the sort of factual findings that the Chamber used to find the underlying act of genocide under Article 4(2)(B), and our position is that the Chamber was reasonable on -- in making those findings. Moving quickly to question number 2. The Trial Chamber -- the question is whether the Trial Chamber erred in finding that the Bosnian Serb forces killed the three Bosnian Muslim leaders from Zepa with the specific intent to destroy part of the Bosnian Muslim population as such. In short, our answer is the Trial Chamber did not err. The Trial Chamber correctly noted that as a general matter when the groups' leadership is targeted for destruction and the remaining members is subject to heinous acts, such as their forced displacement, then the combination of those acts is indicative of the perpetrators' genocidal intent. I refer you to judgement paragraph 777 and 781 and footnote 3138. And when the perpetrators target the core of the group for destruction and displace the remaining members, those acts, taken together, demonstrate the intent to destroy the group by preventing it even -- from even the residual possibility of reconstituting itself. And these are concepts found in the Jelisic trial judgment paragraph 82 and the Krstic appeals judgement paragraph 31. And with this law in mind, the Trial Chamber analysed what happened in Zepa. The leadership of the Zepa community was targeted for destruction because of their importance to the community and they were -- and the remaining Bosnian Muslims were subject to other heinous acts such as their mass displacement. The combined effect of these acts was aimed at ensuring the population of the Zepa enclave would not be able to reconstitute itself in turn demonstrating that the Bosnian Serb forces acted with genocidal intent. The Chamber's analysis is in paragraph 774 to 782. I think I will stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So you are saying, Mr. Kremer, that the killing of those three persons was an essential element in preventing the group from reconstituting itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: It was evidence from which the Chamber could infer -- it was evidence of an underlying act of genocide, which the killing is, and it was evidence from which the Chamber could infer, in light of all of the circumstances, that it was done with genocidal intent. And the analysis that the Chamber did was to attempt to articulate, as fully as possible, the basis upon which it made that determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Isn't this a case in which you would have to be satisfied that this is the only inference that could be drawn?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If it is -- can you reasonably say that this is the only inference that could be drawn?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: There is a -- I -- I say that the only -- the conclusion, the legal conclusion hasn't been proven beyond a reasonable doubt that Tolimir had genocidal intent is a question that is beyond a reasonable doubt determination. And if it's a circumstantial case totally, then it must be the only reasonable conclusion. The reasonable inference issue that -- I think there is a mix-up among legal officers and perhaps even Judges of this Tribunal, the -- the only reasonable inference concept goes to fact finding. And if there is a -- a factual finding that is made that relies on only circumstantial evidence, then it must be the only reasonable inference. But the conclusion at the end of the day as to the guilt or innocence on the essential elements is one of reasonable doubt, and if it's a circumstantial case, totally, then it must be the only reasonable conclusion. And ultimately, the test on appeal is was the decision -- was the conclusion as to guilt reasonable. That's -- that's my submission. You cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yeah, but I think I agree with you that there is a confusion. Well, in the instant case, I agree with you the ultimate question is beyond reasonable doubt, you know, but before you get to that question don't you have a number of issues that go to the evidence which the Prosecution is relying on to prove intent? I mean, that happens in any case --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- where you have to prove intent and that is usually done on the basis of inferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And when you look at the judgement, the Chamber looked at, and particularly in the genocide section, it -- it drew a lot of inferences. And it -- when it's making factual findings relating to a variety of things in these paragraphs, it -- it is actually saying -- and the only reasonable inference was that, well, and then there is the factual finding, and then there is the next factual finding, many of which are based on reasonable inference. Some are based on reasonable doubt. I have no -- the Chamber has no doubt that this is the fact. But at the end of this finding, and this is different than the JCE to murder, the Chamber actually finds that this is the only reasonable conclusion. That's what it says. It may even mistakenly say "inference," but our submission is that the -- at the end of the day the final conclusion is not an inference one, it's based on -- based on all of the findings whether, properly made, is the -- is the Chamber satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused committed the crime or that the Prosecution has proven the essential elements of the crime so that the conviction can be registered. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It cannot be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt if it made a mistake in assessing a question of inference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I agree with that too. But the only thing that falls away is the inference. You still then are saying, Okay, without that inference or without that finding, what's left. And everything else that's left may still lead to the same result. It doesn't mean that the world all of a sudden falls off the pedestal because there are multiple legs holding up the finding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but it becomes more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: It may or may not, depends on how many findings there are and how substantial they are. And this is a case where there is a wealth of evidence carefully, carefully analysed that deserves a careful consideration by this Chamber as to if something doesn't satisfy you, a factual finding, to look at what's left and determine whether that still supports the ultimate conclusion. The ultimate conclusion should not fall because of one little fact. Unless you've got any further questions, Your Honour, I'll conclude my remarks. Mr. Wood will deal with the alternative modes of responsibility. And on his behalf, because I've used so much time answering your questions, perhaps being more wordy than I have been, if you would give him five more minutes, I'm sure he'd appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We will. You have ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. The answer, Your Honours, to question 5, is, yes, General Tolimir can be held liable for his role in the Srebrenica killings under the other modes of responsibility that have been charged in the indictment at paragraph 66. I've prepared my presentation to go in order of the modes that the Prosecution believes are most relevant. You've heard a lot about the contributions today to the JCE to murder. Those contributions, as I can explain, also support a finding that he ordered the crimes or that he can be held responsible as an orderer, as an instigator, as a planner, and that he can also be held responsible for commission by omission, and of course aiding and abetting. The Prosecution believes that the evidence shows that ordering, planning, instigating, are the primary modes that, if Your Honours should turn away from JCE, that those are the modes you should look at because the evidence shows that he was so deeply involved in the murder operation that that's -- that's the conclusion that you should reach. However, since Your Honour Judge Meron has asked a question about aiding and abetting and considering the time we have left, I'll start with aiding and abetting, if that pleases Your Honours. Now, the Chamber defines the elements of aiding and abetting at paragraphs 907 to 911 of the judgement. So considering everything you've heard about his contributions to the JCE to murder, at the very least, Your Honours, General Tolimir also aided and abetted murder and that he rendered practical assistance, encouragement, or moral support which had a substantial effect on the perpetration of murder and, of course, the other crimes with which he's been charged. He knew that this crime would probably be committed and he knew that his acts would probably assist in its commission. The Prosecution has listed, of course, the contributions that the Chamber found that Tolimir made to the joint criminal enterprise to murder at paragraph 234 of its response brief. I'll highlight just a few of those and they may sound familiar from what you've heard previously. The Chamber found that Tolimir "started actively being involved in the accomplishment of the murder plan" from the moment he came to know about it, at the latest by the 13th of July. That's the Chamber's finding at paragraph 1104. The Chamber found that through his continued involvement in concealing the murder operation as it unfolded and his failure to protect the Bosnian Muslim prisoners, Tolimir helped ensure that the murder operation would unfold smoothly, secretly, and uninterrupted. That's at paragraph 1164 of the judgement. The Chamber also found that Tolimir "directed, controlled, and supervised his subordinate organs and personnel" throughout the murder operation including such men as Popovic, Salapura, Jankovic, his direct subordinate Beara, as was Salapura, and Keserovic. As the Chamber found, as you've heard today, each of these men was deeply and extensively involved in the murder operation. All of these efforts, Your Honours, helped ensure that the operation would be successful, and they amounted to a lot of other acts -- a lot of other ways, modes of responsibility. But at the very least, Your Honours, they amounted to a substantial contribution to the resulting crimes. Now as to General Tolimir's mens rea, it remains the Prosecution's case that the Trial Chamber was correct in finding that he did have genocidal intent and that he did have the intent to commit each of the crimes with which he was convicted by the Trial Chamber. That aside, Your Honours, as to the mens rea for aiding and abetting, the Chamber's finding showed that he continued to deliberately fail to act despite his knowledge that his subordinates were extensively involved in a murder operation, a murder operation that was being carried out with genocidal intent and murder operation that was being carried out with a persecutory content, a murder operation on a massive scale. This shows that Tolimir knew that these crimes would probably be committed by the direct perpetrators at the very least and that his acts would probably assist in their commission. And I'll point out one final thing as to aiding and abetting, Your Honours. The Chamber also found that an accused can be held responsible for -- can aid and abet a crime by providing tacit approval and encouragement, and that's at paragraph 909. And if you recall, Your Honours, the Chamber found that Tolimir tacitly approved the murders at the Branjevo military farm and at Bisina, both of which were perpetrated by units under his command and supervision as the 10th Sabotage Detachment. Based on all of these findings, Your Honours, Tolimir can be convicted for aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation, and execution of the indictment crimes. And with the time I have left, I'll focus on ordering, Your Honours. And let me just say, the Prosecution will brief these matters if Your Honours would find that useful so we can spell it out more plainly and in perhaps longer form. So as to ordering, the Chamber found -- defined the elements of ordering at paragraphs 904, 906 of the judgement. They also found that Tolimir was providing -- "providing guidance, instructions, and orders to his subordinates who were sending him up-to-date information." That's at paragraph 1125. Now this included, of course, Beara, and it includes Popovic. Beara was his direct subordinate. Popovic was a man who he controlled through the professional chain of command. As the Chamber found, these men helped to implement, co-ordinate, and supervise the murder operations in the Zvornik area. They also helped to supervise the burial and reburial operations. That's at paragraph 1064 and 1066. There are a couple of orders that are -- instructions that show that Tolimir was in constant contact with them. As you've heard from Mr. Kremer, on the 14th, Tolimir issued a telegram alerting the Drina Corps of the presence of unmanned aircraft and he ordered them to shoot it down if they see it. And as you've heard in today's hearing, on the 22nd of July, General Tolimir had a conversation with Popovic in which he told him, "You just do your job." Now what's important about this, Your Honours, is the date. The Chamber found this happened on the 22nd of July. At this moment General Tolimir knew, the Chamber found, that Popovic had been deeply involved in the murder operation that had been unfolding for at least ten days. And, of course, the Chamber found that the very next day Popovic supervised the 10th Sabotage Detachment in the killing of at least 39 Bosnian Muslim men in Bisina. That's at 976. There is similar evidence to show, Your Honours -- not evidence, let me correct that. Findings from the Chamber that show -- or findings in the judgement that support a finding that Tolimir can be held responsible as a planner, as an instigator, and by commission by omission. And as I said, I don't have time to get into those but I'm happy to brief those for Your Honours if you wish. Let me just wrap up, Your Honours, by saying the Prosecution's position remains, as you heard from Mr. Kremer today, that this is a JCE case. The Chamber found that the murder operation resulted in the systemic murder of at least 5.749 Bosnian Muslims, most of them in the 72 hours between the 13th of July and the 16th of July, 1995. Like any successful and complicated military operation, they required the shared intent and significant contribution of dedicated individuals including Tolimir and men that he commanded and that he controlled. But it was also a vast military operation, Your Honours. Military operations run on plans and they run on orders. The Chamber's findings show that Tolimir and his subordinates were essential players to the successful execution of this particular operation, the murder operation. As such, though Tolimir is properly described as having committed the crimes as a member of a JCE, he can also be held liable for murder under each of these alternate modes of liability that the Prosecution charged in paragraph 66 of the indictment. And that -- without going into the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just wondered whether you would very briefly expand on commission by omission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'd be happy to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And perhaps I was confused. I'm not sure about how much additional time, if any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You have two minutes for commission by omission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, I would guide Your Honours to paragraph 1 -- 1117 and footnote 3528 of the judgement to show the elements of comission by omission. And I'll go through those elements briefly. So essentially the Chamber found that Tolimir had a duty to protect the prisoners, that he was duty-bound to comply with the laws that included the Geneva Conventions. That's at paragraph 1121. He was also obligated to protect the prisoners under domestic criminal law and under his own VRS rules and regulations, and these are at paragraphs 1118 to 1121 of the judgement. Secondly, General Tolimir had the ability to fulfil his duty. Now, the findings are legion to support this, Your Honour. In fact, the Chamber found that "the evidence casts no doubt on the material ability" of General Tolimir to protect the Bosnian Muslim prisoners from Srebrenica. And that's at 1126 of the judgement. Now, as you've heard, General Tolimir played at the central role at matters concerning POW exchanges. That's at Chamber finding at 1122. And this is borne out by other evidence and findings, Your Honours. Recall that it was Tolimir who told Milenko Todorovic to prepare the Batkovic detention centre for the prisoners. That's at paragraph 931. And it was Tolimir who told him the prisoners aren't coming, that's at 951. Now this is evidence, Your Honours, of the power that General Tolimir had as the security and intelligence chief in dealing with prisoners of war and prisoners. And finally, Tolimir failed to exercise his duty to protect the prisoners, and these findings - I would guide Your Honours to paragraph 1126 of the judgement - they listed the things that General Tolimir could have done but failed to do, such as direct his subordinates to comply with the rules governing the treatment of prisoners. He could have confronted Mladic, a man over whom he'd had an amount of influence about what was unfolding, and he could have reported the crimes that he knew were happening to the military prosecutors. And the Chamber found that he took none of these steps and that his failure to protect the prisoners resulted in their murders. And in this way, Your Honours, he can be held responsible for commission by omission. Although, I'll say once again the Prosecution believes JCE is the primary way in which he's responsible. And then as an orderer, as an instigator, and as a planner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Wood, for your response. We will meet at 4.35. 4.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Before turning to the counsel for Mr. Tolimir for his reply of 20 minutes, I understand that the Prosecution would like to make a very brief corrections to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Something I'm told which requires two minutes -- three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Two minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: -- hopefully at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Go ahead. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, Mr. President, but on the B/C/S channel I'm hearing French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You see, we are ecumenical [Realtime transcript read in error "economical"]. Can the Registry help Mr. Gajic's technological problems, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, the technical problem seems to have been resolved. I can hear Serbian in my headset and I read English on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see in the transcript my word "ecumenical" was transcribed as "economical" which is really not quite the same, is it? And, right. Well, it is -- now, my correction on the record. I hope that you will see it on the record. My word "economic" -- after my word there is a missing word, "ecumenical." Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. On page 56 I misspoke two times, apparently. I meant to say paragraphs "1099 to 1028 of the judgement" -- or, I'm sorry, 1128. I misspoke again. On page 64, I meant to say "transcript 12942," not "12492." On page 65 I meant to say "Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility," not "Zvornik area of responsibility." On page 74, line 22, I meant to say "P488," not "paragraph 488." On page 94 line 4, Mr. Wood meant to say "continued to deliberately act and failed to act" not just "failed to act." And on page 95, line 21, Mr. Wood left out a citation, it should have been judgement paragraph 1165. And finally on P68, line 18, I stated "Bosnian Muslim men and boys who had just been executed en masse." That should read "captured Bosnian Serb soldiers." That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now a reply by Mr. Gajic for Mr. Tolimir. You are supposed to speak 30 minutes, but since we gave an extra five minutes to the Prosecution we will give you an extra five minutes. So you have 35 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you again. As for corrections to the transcript, I will also have to make some. But I'm not able to do so now. I will have to listen to the audio recording first. I hope that will be very soon.
