In its reply, the Prosecution presented quite a few matters contained in the judgement giving their reasoning including some positions that are inacceptable to the Defence. The Defence believes that the Trial Chamber did not establish these matters properly. One of the issues that are perhaps key in this case concerns the position of Mr. Tolimir in the Main Staff of the VRS and the system of command and control. Whether the others mentioned by the Prosecution Nikolic, Carkic, Trbojevic, and others were subordinated to Tolimir, the Defence believes not. They were not subordinated to Tolimir. Tolimir was not their commander. Tolimir was an assistant commander and they acted as part of their own units and they were subordinated to their own commanders at the level of the corps to the corps commander, at the level of brigade to the brigade commander. This is shown clearly, among other things, by Exhibit P2609, signed by Commander Ratko Mladic, which states -- it's a document dated 13 January, 1995: "The sections of security should organisationally be subordinated directly to the commander, and according to the professional line directly to the Main Staff of the VRS, whereas intelligence sections should be organisationally subordinated to the chiefs of staff with the proviso that the work of the narrow circle of command should include them in making decisions for action. Professionally intelligence sections are linked to the intelligence department of the Main Staff of the VRS." What does the professional line imply? It does not imply command. It implies appropriate professional training, direction, guidance, how to perform certain tasks in order to have it done uniformly in the entire Army of Republika Srpska. I will read a part of the same document that I just mentioned, 2609, to see what the role of Tolimir was. Tolimir does not command them. What is Tolimir doing? It is said in this document, among other things, that all those who are supposed to communicate with UNPROFOR or anyone outside the VRS such as foreign armies, et cetera, should undergo interviews and appropriate procedures with security and intelligence organs to receive assignments, whether it concerns gathering of intelligence or something else, whereas the chief of the Main Staff of the VRS, in this case Tolimir, says "shall with a special instruction regulate powers, competencies, and the method of preparing such persons." That is his assignment. In our appeals brief, we cited the evidence of Witness Colic who during the war was a brigade commander throughout the war. What did he have to say about the security organs in the higher command vis-à-vis the security organs in the lower command. I cite: [In English] "Only in terms of professional education." [Interpretation] That there is no relationship between security organs at various levels is said by the same witness and that is in keeping with all the other evidence led in this case, and he says all the orders follow the system of command, whereas security organs from the lower command do not receive orders from the higher command. It's on pages 19278 through 12 -- 19279. The same witness also talked about Tolimir's behaviour. Tolimir never wanted to impose himself as someone from the Main Staff. He was always prepared to listen and to propose the best solutions. But in order not to humiliate them, he never issued orders to the security organ from his unit or any other unit. So Tolimir is not the one who commanded security organs. He doesn't even command intelligence organs. He is a professional who provides appropriate instructions. Then another Prosecution exhibit, P1112, specifies the tasks of the security organ from the higher commands relative to the security organs in lower commands. They monitor professionalism and regularity and lawfulness in work, but this control is not something that is carried out at the moment a certain task is carried out. Security organs are autonomous. That control, that inspection is periodical, whether annual or quarterly, et cetera. The Prosecution views the whole matter through the prism of killings in Srebrenica. We have to remember it's not a systemic operation that took place over two or three years. It lasted only a few days. We understand the effort of the Prosecution to narrow everything down to those killings, but everything that was organised was organised during those few days. The plan for the murders, as established by the Trial Chamber, did not exist before the enclave of Srebrenica was captured. Furthermore, the Prosecution mentioned the very close relationship between Tolimir and Mladic. Mr. Tolimir never contested that during the trial and of course we are not going to contest it now. Everybody in the Main Staff had to be close to Mladic. But to take that as a prism through which all the evidence is viewed, that Tolimir was Mladic's eyes and ears, it's just a metaphor for the functional of intelligence and security organs. Nothing more than that. The witness who stated that was the chief of staff, number two in the Main Staff of the VRS, deputy commander. The Prosecution refers to the evidence of Milenko Todorovic, that is to the adjudicated fact that allegedly on 12 July Tolimir let Todorovic know that he should prepare the Batkovic camp for the arrival of prisoners. First of all Todorovic, and I will point out references in the appeal brief paragraph 356, Milenko Todorovic cannot remember exactly who communicated to him that the Batkovic camp should be prepared to accommodate POWs. Here in the courtroom in order to show him whose authority it was, whose duty it was to do that, we showed him a document from 1993, and Milenko Todorovic, and the Trial Chamber failed to evaluate the behaviour of the witness in the courtroom who was obviously relieved, Milenko Todorovic said, "Thank God we finally see the document which we have been discussing at such length." The document was signed chief of staff -- Chief of the Main Staff of the VRS. Furthermore, when Tolimir told Todorovic that the prisoners would not be arriving, the Prosecution says it was at the latest on the 13th, using that to corroborate their theory that on the 13th Tolimir was aware of the killings. However, Todorovic cannot remember the date, whether it was the 14th or the 15th or the 16th. And the argument of the Defence is that Todorovic was not telling the truth about this, and that is shown by the evidence of Novica Simic as cited in paragraph 358 of our appeal brief. Novica Simic in the Popovic et al. case said truthfully who called him, who he talked to, and who gave him which information. He doesn't even mention the conversation between his security organ and Tolimir. I have to express my regret here that we did not manage to test Todorovic's evidence by hearing Novica Simic's evidence because Novica Simic died in the meantime. There is a reference to this in paragraph 358 and 359 of our appeal brief. Also speaking of P2069. Did Tolimir know about the separation? It's a document that says that military-age able-bodied men were separated at Potocari, about 70 of them. It's a document dated the 12th. In the upper part of the document, there are initials of all those who read the document. Tolimir's initials are not among those. Furthermore, that Tolimir did not see this document is shown by D64, where Tolimir insists that all military-age able-bodied men who are being evacuated from the base at Potocari should be listed and registered. So Tolimir believes they should fair the same as all the other civilians evacuated from Potocari instead of being held. In the presentation of the Prosecution, many issues were raised about the situation in Zepa. Was there a genocide in Zepa? Was the operation carried out with a certain genocidal intent? Were civilians targeted? Were they exposed to suffering? There is not a single piece of evidence showing that there was a genocide in Zepa or that the operation in Zepa was carried out with any genocidal intent. That inference can be made only if one speculates through the murder operation. And even when the Prosecution views that murder operation beginning with Srebrenica, they suppose that everybody is acting in a common purpose, jointly, as they always do under the rules. However, from the description given in the judgement, we see the following: Is Beara talking to Tolimir when he's facing problems in the assignments given him, or is he talking to Krstic and Zivanovic? He communicates with the people who are in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps. Tolimir is in Zepa. Why would they inform Tolimir? It is indeed the duty of security organs to monitor whether a crime has been committed somewhere and to file criminal complaints, but that's the job of the security department. It's not Tolimir who is supposed to run around and control this. Were the security organs really functioning properly? I would say not. From the position regularly occupied by Tolimir, one cannot draw the inference that he is equally involved in the criminal activity. Furthermore, the issue is raised here why those able-bodied military-aged men in Zepa were not killed. The Prosecution says because they had run away to Serbia, for instance. But let us see what happened in Zepa from the beginning. The moment Tolimir arrives in Zepa, he gives them a choice: Lay down your arms, those who want to stay in Zepa may; those who don't want to stay may leave. There are negotiations on the 13th, 19th, 24th, 27th of July. UNPROFOR is there. The proposal is made to place them under the supervision of the ICRC and UNPROFOR pending an exchange of prisoners of war. Is there any genocidal intent there or an intent to kill them? A correct version of the events in Zepa was given by a Prosecution witness, Viktor Bezruchenko in D55. As soon as the Defence identified this exhibit, it tendered it. It's an excellent document speaking volumes about the actual unfolding of events. It describes all the machinations that took place with the surrender of weapons in Zepa. Avdo Palic came to negotiate that. There was a dilemma whether an agreement was reached or not, and then they transferred to Serbia. There is no evidence that they were killed or that anybody planned to kill them. That theory can only be pure speculation and nothing more than that. The Prosecution also invokes Exhibits P2875 and P122. These exhibits show one instruction, one proposal by Tolimir. How does the OTP interpret that? Don't register them because they need to be killed. However, these documents clearly say they should not be registered in case the Muslims violate the agreement that had been reached. And it says explicitly: We will save them for an exchange. There is no mention of the possibility that any of them could or should be killed. There was a proposal, let me remind you, that they would be placed under the supervision of the UNPROFOR pending an exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] They would not be registered, correct? Is that what you said? So if the -- should the Muslims violate the agreement, then they would not be registered?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what we read in the document: In case they violated the agreement, they should not be registered and that they should be kept there for future exchanges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But if they are in a limbo of not being registered despite the clear obligation under the Third Geneva Convention to register them, then isn't it fair for the Prosecution also to say that this may have some much more ominous consequences?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If we look at the document, in the document itself it says that they will be guarded for an exchange. Second of all, I would like to remind you that the registration of prisoners of war is indeed an obligation pursuant to the Third Geneva Convention. However, non-registering of a prisoner of war could not constitute a serious violation of the Geneva Conventions. This certainly cannot fall into the category of serious violations. If they are safe-guarded but not registered, that doesn't mean that they will be killed. We saw that there were a lot of problems with regard to an agreement as to how prisoners of war would be exchanged, according to what principle prisoners of war were to be exchanged for Serbian prisoners of war. But there were a lot of delays and problems in that. These two documents certainly cannot be used as proof of a genocidal intent or any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: It seems to me that if you would want to exchange prisoners of war, registering would be a preliminary step which would fit into exchange, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this particular situation -- or rather, in normal situations of course the answer would be yes. However, the situation as it prevailed in Zepa and the problems that existed there were negotiations were being played with. The Army of Republika Srpska was under a lot of pressure by UNPROFOR with regard to Zepa. They played with the agreements, and the question is whether the Serbian prisoners of war were registered. That's all. We don't have any proof that Serbian prisoners of war were also not registered. We don't have any proof to that fact. Second of all, the status of not being registered, if I'm not mistaken, but we can check in the document, can last only during combat and not after that. That may be a day or perhaps a little bit longer, but not much longer than that. That status of not being registered, according to Tolimir, should have been of a very, very temporary nature, only for the duration of combat activities in order to prevent abuses by the Muslim side. Let's not forget that at that time they already started crossing over to Serbia or they were trying to break through in some other directions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If I come back for a second into the first issue in which you elaborated - namely, the consequences and the nature of being assistant commander - would you agree that at the very least an assistant commander would know everything that is relevant to the commander because he has to help him in doing his job, that he's completely informed about what is going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under regular conditions, yes. However, we have a case here that it wasn't Tolimir who had a say as to what a security organs at lower levels would be doing. We saw a document that I have already mentioned. Let me just try and find the number for you. Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: My question was about knowledge not now about giving orders. I would like now to come to the question of orders. You considered, I think you agree, that an assistant commander would basically know everything that the commander knows. As regarded the capacity, the competence to give orders, imagine that Mr. Tolimir, as assistant commander, deals with those questions we dealt with earlier, accommodation and hangars and so on. Presumably when he talks to senior commanders, he would make it clear that he's acting on behalf of his boss, wouldn't he, and then they would not raise questions about his competence, would they?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to make a little correction on the first question, which is the issue of knowledge. An assistant commander doesn't have to know everything that a commander knows. In the military there is a rule of people being informed on a need-to-know basis. An assistant commander does not have to know everything. A commander can bypass his assistant for any reason. For example, he may have been sent on a mission and the commander doesn't want to disturb him. And as for issuing instructions and orders, we have to make a distinction between two things: One is a normal customary situation, and the other situation is an extraordinary situation, an exceptional different situation of the kind that existed during this operation to kill, the murder operation that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: That was not the -- a minor thing. That was the biggest thing that was happening. Is it conceivable that the assistant commander would not know about that? That would somewhat stretch the imagination, wouldn't it, that he would not know about what's going on with regard to killing of thousands of people?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, when we speak about this specific situation, Tolimir was sent to Zepa on Mladic's order. Beara, the chief of the security administration, was in Srebrenica on the other hand. Commander Mladic sent other security and intelligence men to various missions in the area of responsibility of either the Bratunac Brigade or the Zvornik Brigade, and he never seeks Tolimir's approval for any of that. It is quite possible to notice that the assistant commander for security and intelligence was really not informed about certain things. At that time, as shown by documents, Tolimir was engaged in Zepa first and foremost, and developments in Zepa were by no means simple. There were a lot of negotiations. They had to cross very difficult terrain and spent time in Zepa without any communications there. Why would anybody inform Tolimir in the first place if Tolimir was not involved in the whole thing? I'm not going to tackle other things at this moment; i.e., whether somebody from the Main Staff participated in that or not. Our position has always been that members of the Main Staff are separate cases and those separate cases are heard separately. To put it simply: Tolimir was simply not there, not in those situations. Let me remind the Appeals Chamber - I can see that I have two more minutes left - of a decision or a dissenting opinion by Judge Badawi Pasha in the Corfu Channel case. He was considering a second-hand evidence and he pointed to the danger of interpreting that evidence where voids are filled with various assumptions, associations, and that certainty cannot be achieved in that way. The standard of proof that has to be achieved before this Tribunal is not probability or likelihood or reasonability of a decision but rather a high degree of certainly beyond any reasonable doubt. In this case, the Prosecutor has not succeeded to prove beyond reasonable doubt that Tolimir was aware of the murder operation, that he was a participant in that operation, or that he intended to participate in the murder operation. Therefore, we believe that he should be acquitted on all counts of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel, for your argument. This brings us to the end of arguments by the parties. And now the time has come to ask Mr. Tolimir whether he would like to exercise his right of ten minutes personal statement. THE APPELLANT: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Microphone. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] I would like to address the Trial Chamber with a few words. With your leave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Appeals Chamber. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Appeals Chamber, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please do. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet all the members of the Appeals Chamber, all the interpreters, and the staff of Tribunal, the Prosecutor's office, and the Defence, and all the other personnel that has helped us during the trial and enabled us to finish the trial without any technical problems. The Prosecutor's Office as a segment of this Tribunal says that Tolimir should be sentenced based on the Prosecutor's conclusions which are not based on evidence but rather on assumption as well as on the erroneous translation of documents with decisions that were never implemented on the destruction of any individual or groups of individuals either in Zepa or in other parts of the territory of Republika Srpska. Also, those tasks were not implemented in terms of the disputable "zbegovi." Those proposals were never realised about those, "zbegovi." I don't know why in these proceedings this programme referring to zbegovi has been mistranslated both in French and in English as well as in Serbian, although that term or the terms that are used in all the three languages are identical. Why have they been translated in an identical way in all the three languages? Was the document translated from English into French? I don't know. But the Appeals Chamber should establish that, why the difference in the translations as referred to by Judge Antonetti. It will be my honour to be sentenced based on the interpretations and descriptions proffered by the Prosecutor here today as well as based on the erroneous translation of documents about the destruction of natural features in mountains outside of settlements and outside of the range of the weapons of the Army of Republika Srpska and contrary to the provisions on the authorities of the accused in combat and through a different application of the evidence on the part of the Prosecution both during my trial and during the hearing today. Also, I would like to say that there are very different interpretations on the part of the Prosecutor and on the part of the Trial Chamber on the role of the sides of the conflicts; i.e., the VRS on the one hand and the BiH Army on the other hand. In a demilitarised zone under the control of UNPROFOR, attacks were launched from there on the territory of Republika Srpska against the population, the military, even the command post, and those were sabotage attacks by the BiH against the VRS. We tendered evidence to that effect during the trial. There were a lot of such actions. Even Avdo Palic mentioned ten sabotage groups that attacked the forward command post in Han Pijesak, when about 50 members were killed. That was the reason why attacks from Zepa and Srebrenica were repelled when they launched the attacks on the features and facilities of the Army of Republika Srpska outside of Srebrenica and Zepa. I find it surprising that we are being charged with what we were supposed and duty-bound to do and defend by law. We were duty-bound to defend Republika Srpska. It was a legitimate activity. It was our military activity, legitimate activity during combat. However, a month after combat activities in Srebrenica and Zepa, there was a military retaliation against the Army of Republika Srpska and the entire territory of Republika Srpska, including the population and the military on the order of NATO and UNPROFOR. And both were supposed to protect equally Serbs and non-Serbs, all the sides to the conflict in other words. It was a retaliation as was said by General Rupert Smith, the then commander of UNPROFOR, and that's what he said in response to my questions during his testimony. He said that Zlovrh, the highest peak near Zepa, 30 days after the Muslim population of Zepa had left, was bombarded in retaliation. However, the centre where ten soldiers were killed at the time, communications, signalsmen had been destroyed before the aggression of NATO, the Republic of Croatia, the Army of Republika Srpska. Before the NATO aggression, that centre was destroyed. The NATO, the BiH Army, and the Army of Republika Srpska attacked the Army of Republika Srpska [as interpreted]. From that facility, signals were sent to all units in the territory of Republika Srpska, the Republika Srpska of Serbian Krajina, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I am referring only to the well known data about those things familiar to the Trial Chamber, the Appeals Chamber, all the inhabitants of Republika Srpska, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the Republic of Serbian Krajina and all the republics of the former Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. That happened towards the end of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The NATO aggression against Serbia was led by the same person who led the NATO aggression against Republika Srpska. The NATO aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was under the command of the chief of staff of the Supreme Command of NATO in Brussels who at the time of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the UNPROFOR commander, I'm talking about General Rupert Smith. During the preparation for the aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, all the centres in Republika -- of Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska were destroyed as well as in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, including TV centres which showed images of what was going on in the territory of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina as well as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia when it came to NATO aggression. Unfortunately, due to the NATO aggression against the centre and studio that broadcast news of what NATO did during the aggression, the director of the studio was sentenced to ten years in prison and 22 employees of the centre were killed. That centre broadcast shows and they were bombarded based on the signals that they broadcast. The images is something that everybody in the territory of the former SFRY is familiar. There is evidence of that bombardment in this case as well. It was tendered towards the end of my trial. During the aggression of the NATO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I gave you ten minutes. I give you one more minute to sum up, please. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you. When it comes to the NATO aggression against the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I provided evidence during my trial. However, everybody knows about all that, the Trial Chamber, the Appeals Chamber, the population, and all the participants in this trial. These facts will remain as evidence of the happenings which happened exactly in the way I described them. If there is something not true to what I am telling, I am prepared to bear responsibility and stand trial for that. But it is my duty to say that various and different criteria have been applied to various sides to the conflict because of the partiality of NATO commanders, UNPROFOR commanders, and all the relevant international structures which were engaged in the former Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. Thank you. I apologise for overstepping my time. I would like to thank you for allowing me to finish in the way I did in view of the fact that I have nothing written before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Tolimir. This concludes the hearing of the appeal in this case. Before we adjourn, let me just take a moment to thank the parties for their work on this case and for their arguments today. I would like also to express my gratitude to the Registry staff here in the courtroom who have so ably facilitated our hearing today and to the interpreters for their excellent assistance. The Appeals Chamber will render its judgement in due course. The proceedings are adjourned.
